title: Codeine EP
content:
Ethereal sounds, straight from my aesthetic ideology. A cross between an angel high on opiates (hence the title) and a computer trying to take over the world.

Download the entire EP here, or click each individual track name below. All are encoded in 320kbps mp3 format, thought if you are interested I could quite easily produce FLAC/lossless versions. They are inherently designed sonic textures which are almost pointless to listen to unless you're listening through a decent pair of headphones which can reproduce the different bass frequencies or, better still, a great pair of speakers with a heavy sub-woofer.



Track #1: The Right Direction.
Literally, my music heading in the right direction. Quite easily one of my favourite tracks, if not vying for the top spot with blatch.
5:21

Track #2: Lost in the Jungle.
A rather delicious bassline, I think, layered with chirpy synths and an undulating beat.
3:28

Track #3: Freshers.
A short track I made during my university freshers week (possibly the first night) -- heavily experimental.
0:24

Track #4: An Aphorism for a Break.
Glitch heavy.
6:05

Track #5: I Don't Do Labels.
A track which speaks as to my opinion on labels. The ending, particularly, is deliciously unlabelable.
7:14

Track #6: Sepulchral.
The majestic crescendo of my first thought-out and inter-connected EP. I think it brings together all of the themes of the EP in its extended, ten minute expose. I love songs that are seven minutes and above -- truly experimental music.
10:14

title: vds
The Human Condition (poem)
content:
Quantify success, for I calculate
That any answer has no telling trait.
One man's hell can be another's lover --
So show me one who will thus discover

Any universal and agreed stick
To measure joy that is not a vain trick.
The doubt which follows leads many astray,
And though I wish for nothing but to stay.

Past success cannot sustain happiness --
But tragedy follows any excess:
Where lies the balance, where sits perfection?
If I'm right, in introspection.

To accept one's flaws is a kind blessing
But one which requires a life of stressing.
We did not sign up, but we choose
To continue -- no one wishes to lose

This chance to breathe, exist and empathise --
Regardless of the times we despise.
As life goes on, so does evolution --
The human condition: no solution.

title: To England in Spring (sonnet)
content:
The skies alive with ecstasy and light --
Emotion reigns and rings with summer's tint.
The sun in bloom, the season strong and bright:
A look above leads one to smile and squint.
And thus this love of life swells to blooming
Aligned to nature's growth. As old persona
Shatters, the darkness which was once a-looming
Assumes the face of grace known as Verona:
Escaping England -- Summer's surest gift!
I question why, when clouds reveal their pearl:
The beauty present could no English shift
From here, as spring, indeed, does thus unfurl.
The land itself recites the national song;
Throughout it all, I feel that I belong.

title: Combustion Triangle (poem)
content:
Sorrow, anger, self-belief
Mortal ties with no relief.
Fight the way, resist the numb
Suffer, for the night will come.
Dusk permits suspension of talk --
Follow still the thoughts that stalk.
Times of wrenched smiles lack the jolt
Brought by life. Appended bolt
Lies for sake of grace desired:
Skills no poet once admired.

Fighting labels to be free
Taken from the bourgeoisie:
Fitting in or standing out?
Questions soothe the once devout --
Media lies may trick most;
Answers quickly lead to boast --
Boasting gives to sore regret...
Never let them crimes forget.
Shuffled pride can well provide
Doubts -- but don't you dare reside.

This is not the master plan --
Just a flame that I can fan.

title: Mind Moves (sonnet)
content:
The mind moves not in any steady fashion,
At times a stagnant remnant of the past
Quite neutered by pointless compassion—
New notes hidden by the tails of the last,
Fading mournfully, inaccessible
To all but memory; yet life remains
Pregnant to the bright and irrepressible.
Passion o’er all, but delicacy sustains
The greatest growth. Lurches move us forward;
Only on reflection do we understand
Quite who we were; by then, of course, bordered
And barred—never quite at our own command.
For life is lived as though it were a race
Yet it is only ourselves that we chase.

title: La Retraite (Or, The Retreat) (short story)
content:
La Retraite


By Luke Labern


I


He stepped off the train and pulled his cap forward, so as to shade his eyes.

His worn boots made a slight tap as he walked across the large, sun-dried paving stones of the platform, though the noise was subsumed into the general hum of the people present. The train itself was still whistling slightly, as steam continued to rise into the air above the black locomotive, blending into the heat above. It was an exceptionally hot day; he took off his denim jacket and laid it across his right shoulder, the fingers of his right hand forming a hook.

He cut through the assorted people and made a distinctive figure: he was paler than they were, taller than they were, more isolated than they were. He stood around six-one, a lean figure. What little of him could be seen revealed a taut musculature; he had thin forearms, but the veins crisscrossing hinted at his strength. His upper arms were slightly bigger, but what stood out was the tone of his muscles. No one paid much attention to him, however; they were focused on the departures and the arrivals of their loved ones. Without saying a word, he left the station and followed a dirt track, the dust clinging to his boots and blending in with the chocolate brown of his corduroy trousers.

He kept to the side of the track, often stepping on the grass hanging over the edge where the field met the dried mud—which, after he took his next step, raised slightly, each blade sitting a little, before falling once again, accepting its new position. His white t-shirt gradually became saturated with sweat; the middle of his wet back held the material in place whilst the lower portions blew gently in the slight wind.

The landscape was flat and open: only the track had any sense of direction. The grass was a particularly brilliant shade of green, the sun now hanging high, feeding it. There were only two clouds in the sky: a huge cumulonimbus inching across so slowly as to appear motionless. Only he seemed to move.

He continued to follow the track, pausing only to readjust the shoulder on which his jacket rested. The sun crawled across the sky; the cloud moved into the distance and the landscape revealed more of itself. More of the same.

Eventually, a little brown dot in the distance revealed itself as a farmhouse.

Approaching the property, he heard a gentle, rhythmic thwack. As he neared the front of the farmhouse, which possessed its own little track to distinguish it form the larger track upon which he had travelled, he spotted the form of someone laying an axe into a tree trunk. The form was blocked off by one of the posts that held the front of the farmhouse’s roof over the porch. He caught a glimpse of long blonde hair following the motion of its owner as the form picked up another block of wood to be chopped.

He stopped for the first time to study the property, finding it small and modest. He approached the front of the property and saw a name engraved on the front: ‘Béringer’.

He knocked on the front door.

No one answered.

He paused, considering what to do—but he made no move towards the girl chopping wood, who had not heard his gentle knock. He tried again, and this time heard movement: the sound of feet shuffling accompanied by a knock from inside.

An old man opened the door. ‘Oui?’

‘Do you own this farm?’ The younger man spoke in French.

‘Oui.’ The old man leant desperately on a crude walking stick; he was out of breath. He wore dungarees despite the heat.

‘Are you M. Bérginer?’

M. Béringer nodded, so as to break the monotony of his replies.

The young man asked him, in as few words as possible, if he could lodge at the farm in exchange for work.

As he was in the process of asking this, the wood-chopper stepped onto the porch to her father’s left and asked who the man was in a polite way, though also assessing the nature of the man’s visit. She took her father’s arm.

The man looked at the girl’s face very quickly and noted only that she was exceedingly pretty, possessing a pair of deep blue eyes that perfectly offset her pink lips, before returning his focus to the old man.

The man repeated as much as was necessary, and finished his question.

‘Come inside,’ said M. Béringer.

‘Sit, father,’ said the girl, leading the way inside. The old man acquiesced, slowly and awkwardly lowering himself into a dark green armchair.

‘Would you like anything?’ the girl asked.

‘Non, merci.’ The man took his cap off, exposing a handsome, clean-shaven face. His cheeks were thin, and his chin long—he had a distinctive look, but it was the sort of look one remembered fondly. His skin was a healthy brown, though nothing compared to his hosts’; they lived in the sun. He was merely a visitor. He had short brown hair, as dark as it could have been whilst still remaining brown. The sweat that had accumulated under his cap left his hair sticking to his forehead; he slicked his hair back. His hosts were not put off by this, being used to sweating themselves. Though his good looks were hard to ignore, there was something about him that made it difficult to look away.

The girl was attempting to decipher this very point as she stood to her father’s side, her hands resting in front of her, holding one another. She unconsciously squeezed her left thumb with her right hand, which she always did when lost in thought.

The visitor again raised the question.

‘We do not have much here; only a mattress in a spare room.’

‘That is all I ask,’ he replied. ‘I do not ask for luxury.’

The girl continued to scrutinise his face. She noted his small nose, his almost feminine features, his grey eyes. These she found intriguing in isolation, but together they created a unique composition. When the man looked away from her father to her, she quickly looked away. It was obvious that she had been staring at him.

‘May I ask why you have come here? We are very out of the way.’ M. Béringer again coughed; the girl placed her hand on his shoulder.

‘I came only to work.’

‘We cannot pay you.’

‘I do not ask for payment; I just want to work.’

The girl continued to stare at him. This handsome man, who looked slightly awkward, hunched in an armchair sitting to the right of the father, was too tall for the farmhouse: both the father and his daughter were short—the father around ten inches shorter than the man, the girl at least a foot. But it was not this that drew her attention. It was his eyes. Or, rather, their setting.

The man had many wrinkles—an unusually large amount of deep, prominent emotion. He was almost emotionless at the present moment, but his face told the story of a deeply expressive man. The lighting in the farmhouse was not particularly bright, but she could see that little flecks of dirt had set themselves into the man’s face. There were two distinctive lines drawn into forehead, which, though subtle, became quite apparent when he spoke. Around his eyes, however, there were many more: if one were to consider only his eyes, one would have thought him to have existed for fifty years. His eyes looked as though they had seen many things.

‘We are only a small farm,’ the old man continued; ‘we subsist on what we produce. I am too old; my daughter is forced to do the work.’ The old man smiled sadly. ‘If you can help her, you can stay with us for as long as you like.’

‘Merci.’

‘Sophie, please take our guest—I am sorry; I forgot to ask your name.’

‘Isaac,’ he replied.

‘Sophie, please take Isaac to the spare room.’

She blushed upon hearing her name; she had been considering Isaac—contemplating him. She nodded, quickly turning her head so as too hide her blushed cheeks. ‘This way.’

The farm house was small; it took them only a matter of seconds to reach the other end of the building, through a narrow corridor and into small room with a dressing table and, as described, a small, thin mattress on the floor.

Sophie led him into the middle of the room and turned around, not realising that he was standing right behind her. They found themselves face to face in this cramped room—the brightest in the house, for the window took up most of the width of the wall.

She felt a shiver run through her, quickly followed by a rising feeling of warmth. She found herself looking up at his face, once again looking at his eyes.

He recognised the nature of the encounter immediately and stepped back, but not before instinctively studying her.

Her hair was golden, though a particularly light shade in this light. She had a small face, which was exceedingly pretty: her eyebrows were thin, though her lips were not. Her hair was pinned behind her left ear, which for some reason caught his attention. Her small ear, and the new angle of her face this exposed, led him to pause and study her a second longer than he would have liked. He could see no blemish on her face at all, and her dark blue eyes seemed to penetrate him. Her youth added an extra layer of attractiveness; where he possessed tired wrinkles, she had only taut, untroubled skin.

He felt the same warmth rising up in him.

‘May I shower?’ he asked, seeking a reason to leave her.

‘Y-yes,’ she stuttered, once again feeling her cheeks go hot. ‘Outside.’

II


A second axe was found, and Isaac made it his own.

The ferocity and focus with which he tore through work was something to behold. At first, the two of them took it in turns to chop; hers, a skilful action which used as little energy as possible—his, all power. Her arms were well toned; she had been chopping wood since she was a little girl. She was sixteen now, and had the healthy body of one who lived on hard physical labour and high quality food, cultivated by herself. Perhaps equally importantly, she possessed the glow and confidence of autonomy. She was entirely responsible for her continued existence. Her calm and effective approach to chopping mirrored this: she took each action as the constituent part of a larger project, expending precisely the amount of energy required. Her thoughts were focused not only on the task at hand, but on the bigger picture: the work yet to be done. She was able to chop without breaking a sweat.

He, on the other hand, attacked the job. His swings were violent and reckless. More than a few times he came close to injuring himself, at which Sophie let out a small shriek. She attempted to teach him advanced techniques, but it quickly became apparent that his work was for him a form of catharsis.  He let out barely audible grunts as he made his way through each piece of wood, creating such large arcs with his swing that the sweat he quickly accrued flew in a semi-circle, the droplets illuminated by the sunlight from above. In the background all that could be seen were the endless fields of grass, the dirt track and the perfectly still sky.

Much of the time, Sophie stayed with him. They quickly became easy with one another, neither of them alluding to their first meeting alone—that aspect of their relationship was addressed solely through their eyes. At times, however, Isaac became so consumed by his physical labour that he seemed almost possessed: he would chop one piece of wood and, in the same motion, would reach for the next piece, before attacking that without pause. This was not done fluidly, however. It was done aggressively, and thus awkwardly: it was at these times that it seemed likely that he would swing so wildly as to miss the stump altogether and split his lower leg in half.

Sophie left him at these moments solely because she did not want to see him hurt himself—she did, however, stay within earshot.

After the wood had been chopped, they then tended to the chickens. Sophie was pleased more by companionship than by the division of labour—though that allowed her the time to study this reticent man. She attempted to ask natural questions, phrasing them politely, but Isaac seemed only to want to discuss the work.

‘How long have you been in the region?’ she asked, noticing one of the hens hobbling and tending to it.

‘Not long,’ he replied. ‘What is wrong with her?’

‘Her foot.’ Sophie picked up the hen, which was flapping wildly, and exposed a cut.

‘What’s the procedure?’ he asked matter-of-factly. He spoke seriously, though Sophie was calm.

‘I’ll just keep an eye on her; if she doesn’t improve, we’ll have her for dinner.’

Isaac nodded solemnly.

As they made their way through the various jobs to be undertaken, a pattern emerged. Sophie would attempt to start conversation, but Isaac would dictate the direction: always about the work. He also carried his axe around with him.

‘Why do you carry that axe with you?’

‘I may need it,’ he said, smiling. The lines on his face became striking; Sophie could not help but look, fascinated.

Sophie laughed sweetly. ‘We could share the axe, you know.’

Isaac looked at her in reply, his smile having faded. A feeling of warmth rose up between them once again; he quickly moved on to the next job.

At dinner, the three of them sat around a small table and ate from the produce they had farmed. Sophie served her father.

‘How did you get on?’ the old man asked, in a tone different from that he had used in the beginning.

‘It was excellent,’ Isaac replied. ‘You have a beautiful farm.’

Sophie impulsively looked at him, hearing the word ‘beautiful.’

‘Thank you, Isaac,’ said the old man, taking a mouthful of chicken. ‘I hear you’ve been working very hard.’

Sophie blushed.

‘I hope so; I am certainly clumsy. But I enjoy farming very much.’

The dinner continued, largely in silence: Sophie spoke only to her father. She was tired of trying to engage Isaac in conversation—or, more accurately, she felt too fragile to be ignored once again. She was glad to let her father try; Isaac—perhaps out of respect—replied to all of his questions, though this was likely because they largely concerned practical matters. Isaac seemed very eager to learn the technical side of farming, and agricultural economics.

After dinner, the old man drank wine. Isaac declined, as did Sophie. Isaac took his leave early, and headed to his room after thanking his hosts.

‘Well, what do you think, Sophie? Is he a help?’ The old man’s tone was completely different. The last vestige of formality had been shed.

‘I think he is a great help…’

‘But?’

‘But nothing. He is very able, although he is emotional in his work, rather than practical.’ She paused, thinking about Isaac being in his room—and the time she shared with him there. ‘I enjoy the extra company. It’s been a very long time since there have been three of us here.’

‘I am glad. Although I must say I have missed you today, it is nice to have an extra pair of hands. He’s not very talkative, though, is he?’

Sophie did not reply.

‘We’ll see,’ the old man said, coughing. ‘Now, will you read for me?’

‘Of course, father,’ Sophie said, heading to the bookshelf in order to engage in their traditional reading session. ‘What would you like to read today?’

‘You know my favourite.’

III


The days continued to pass.

The work remained the same; Isaac remained a passionate, rather than pragmatic, worker. He seemed to prefer the physical labour much more than the delicate work; Sophie was quick to notice this and allotted him those jobs which allowed him to expend the energy he seemed driven to use. She continued to attempt to probe him, restoring her energy at night—laying awake for several hours each night, thinking of how odd life was, how it changed without warning; how she could never have predicted her current circumstances; how he literally appeared one day, and changed the structure of her domestic—and emotional—life). Over time, he began to open up emotionally. He responded to her light comments with jokes of his own; he came to know the various animals and they gave them names. Their camaraderie was the primary feature of their relationship: each learned from the other, and they saw one another as peers, rather than strangers.

M. Béringer spent his time inside, though he exerted as much energy as he could to bring himself to the window to watch the interaction of his daughter with their visitor. He perceived well that she was studying Isaac; he could not take his eyes off her own. He was indeed interested in Isaac and his unique approach to work, but his attention always centred upon his daughter. If this young man was not present, he would have been outside with her—or, at least, expecting her regular visit inside. With the visitor, however, he knew that she had a new outlet. He welcomed it. Though he was largely pleased at the experience for her sake, being unable to smile himself when he saw the two of them joking, he felt troubled by the fact Sophie had foregone many social encounters like this for his sake. Isaac’s presence was for him bittersweet—largely because it highlighted his own flaws.

Whilst the two of them spent much of their time jesting, Isaac remained prone to moments of brooding intensity—he would cut short a peal of laughter and clench his jaws as if holding something back. Sophie, at these moments, would let her laughter fade gently. She wondered what was behind the changes in his emotion; wondered why she was not able to fully heal or distract him.

At dinner, too, Isaac began to open up. He and M. Béringer discussed literature and philosophy. Isaac, quite enigmatically, would quote—thus starting conversation—and the old man would give his often curt opinion, at which the three of them would begin laughing. Sophie would watch and listen, for the most part: for her, these matters were not interesting. Isaac was interesting. Who was he, and why was he there?

‘I don’t know where you’ve come from, Isaac—and I know you won’t answer my questions—but I find your love for labour quite fascinating,’ the old man would say. Isaac stayed with them after dinner; as the old man drank wine, he would become quite open. Though Isaac abstained, he opened up too—as if relying on the fact that the old man would remember little of what he said.

Sophie noted that during the day, he would focus his attention on her, whilst at night he would focus on her father. She wondered when he focused on himself.

‘My friend, I love it here. I adore the simplicity of the work. There are no complications: the goals are very simple. You need shelter, you need food: so you work each day to achieve that. You go to sleep each night having achieved that, and you are so tired that you sleep soundly. You wake up the next day and carry on. You are… accompanied by your family, and you face no financial problems. What money you do need you get from selling wood, of which there is an abundance. I can think of very little that I would rather do than live like this until the day I die.’ Isaac became quite passionate; his face revealed pure joy. The lines in his face that revealed themselves only when he smiled became prominent.

‘Although I no longer work—for I am near the end (don’t worry, Sophie!)—I do understand your thinking. I am very tired; it is difficult for me to do the few things I can do. I do, however, remember vividly my working days. I remember growing up a boy, and living in a place very similar to this. My friends were always the animals around me. I mourned their deaths: but I respected them as much as the people I knew. For, though they could not speak, they were the ones who could speak to me through their presence alone. We did not need words.’

Sophie looked at Isaac, and caught him looking at her. For the first time, he did not look away. He continued to look at her, aware that the old man was quite inebriated. He was, however, listening very carefully to his words.

Sophie, with her heart beating rapidly and the palms of her hands moist with sweat, felt her chest heave as they looked at one another.

‘I believe that how one lives says much more about them than what they say. I know you are from England, Isaac: I think people there do more talking than they do acting. We are simple people, but we are happy people.’

‘I couldn’t agree more,’ Isaac said, simply. ‘What I love most about your way of life is what Rousseau would have respected: you are very close to nature, in many respects. I do not think you believe you own this land; you simply cultivate it. I see no intrusion of the state, nor reliance upon it. I see a man and his daughter. I see love, I see respect and I see life. You do not worry about the things I worry about where I come from. And that… makes me love you.’ He clenched his jaws at this revealing phrase. He immediately looked embarrassed, but the old man reached across the table and held Isaac’s hand, squeezing it.

Isaac looked up at him and saw the old man’s simple, smiling face. Neither said a word. He looked at Sophie, who looked surprised—her father, although a kind man, did not display emotion like this. She felt herself well up; as did Isaac.

‘Thank you,’ Isaac whispered, taking his leave.

As emotions once again rose, Isaac left: Sophie realised that this was his reaction to all forms of intensity. His departure did indeed reduce the tension, but it also left a hole where he had been. The father and daughter sat together for a little while, both now reflecting on how life had thrown Isaac their way.

‘Shall I read, father?’ she asked, after a short while.

‘Yes,’ her father replied, wiping something from his eye. ‘Rousseau. A Discourse.’

IV


 The next morning, Sophie brought Isaac a glass of fresh milk and a thick slice of bread for breakfast. She knocked, but heard no reply.

Opening the door, she found he was gone. All that remained was a piece of paper, folded in half and laid on the pillow.

Sophie knew instantly what had happened—although she did not understand why—and felt her hands tremble. She placed the tray she was holding on the floor and picked up the note, which read:

            Thank you for having me.

V


 Isaac stepped onto the train and pulled his cap forward, so as to hide his identity from those who might knew him.

On the train, a solemn-looking woman dressed in a dark blue suit dress handed him a script.

‘You have twenty-four hours to learn your lines. We’ll be in London by tonight.’

title: 3 things I learned at university
content:
Assuming one enters university to improve themselves, perhaps the major question one must ask themselves before making the decision to spend 3+ years in further education is: what will I learn? I leave aside all mention of 'employability' and 'cost'. University is an excellent thing to do if you are unaware of where you stand in life, if you are after one last great send-off to your childhood and teenage years, if you want to experiment without having to worry about 'the real world' and if you love learning. (It won't hurt if you require to do whatever job you're after, of course—but an entrepreneur requires no education, only a mind.) I am talking here about how university improved me as a person and made me better equipped for life. Ironically, much of the leaps in maturity and ability I have made were as a direct result of the flaws of the education I was given. Regardless of how I learned or acquired them, the overall experience of university was undoubtedly something that allowed me to flourish.

So: here are the three most important things I learned at university. As is my aim in all things, I hope that by writing about these things you can learn them for yourself without having to do anything but read this piece and think on the issues at hand. Of course, I still recommend going to university if the stress of constant examination and quantitative grading does not overweigh the positives you stand to gain.

1.Books are the source of wisdom—and will change your life.


I hope the obvious nature of this key fact does not blur you from its importance. I knew, like all of us do, that books contain wisdom. However, like all clichés, the fact that I such a truth was taken for granted stopped me from being able to contemplate it. 

2. You are capable of far more than you thought.


Within the first few weeks of arriving, I was shocked to find that over the course of a 10 week term, I was expected to read 8 novels. 3 years later, I

3. Never accept anyone else's definition of you: define yourself.


Though I almost dropped out...

title: Game of Thrones: are the book better?
content:
In short, no.

I've watched all four series of Game of Thrones and have been making my way through the books after a delay. The delay stems from the fact that I am not a major fan of fantasy writing. The only reason I am reading them is because the torturous nine-month wait between the end of one series and the start of the next is exhausting. What attracts me to the books is the ability to know what will happen in the next season—and thus to marvel at how the story is portrayed on the screen—and because the amorality of the various characters is something that I, like everyone else, finds appealing.

However, when attempting to compare the two, I found that there was no competition. I need only refer you to one phrase from the first book of A Song of Ice and Fire:
"Ser Alliser Thorne walked from the room so stiffly it looked as though he had a dagger up his butt."[1]

That this ever entered the mind of George R. R. Martin—let alone the fact he not only wrote it into a work of art and that it remained after he revised the book—signals why he is not a great writer. There is no doubting his imagination, but his actual ability as a writer is questionable. However, there are clarifications to make. In terms of his being a fantasy writer, I don't think there's any doubting his quality. He writes—for the most part—effectively. He tells his story and moves around his characters at a nice pace. His writing is consistent. His descriptions, whilst necessarily thick due to the escapist tendencies of the fantasy genre, are over-the-top. For many fantasy readers, perhaps they hit the spot. For me, they are distracting. I find myself wading through them hoping to get to dialogue—particularly the dialogue of Tyrion—which is where the series' strength lies.

I find it fascinating that the weaknesses of the TV show don't seem to stem from the weaknesses in the book (though there are exceptions). The excessive nudity and some of the wooden acting are of course relevant only to the TV show. The clichéd setting, coupled with the absurd use of modern words ("fuck", "butt", etc.) are, however, of Martin's own making. They are the reason I have great trouble settling into each season of the show. After a few episodes I can cast off the irritating way characters wearing mud-caked leathers will randomly—and unironically—discuss fucking someone and can enjoy the series' strengths—namely, loathing characters I used to love and loving characters I used to love. Along with Tyrion.

Yes: Tyrion is the best part of Martin's creation, there is no doubt of that. However, once again the TV show pips the books. Though his material is always excellent, Peter Dinklage is the star of the show and carries the show through its lowest moments.

title: Simplicity
content:
Simplicity is the ultimate virtue.

The power of this truth is truly staggering once you allow it to seep into every fibre of your being. Like all truths, it can be hard to really accept it on board. When it is presented to you, it is all too easy to feel that "this is obvious", and that somehow you are already a master of this truth. The idea that every truth we come across—like "work hard", "control your drug use", "make time to calm your mind"—is somehow already a part of us and features in our day-to-day life is one of the parts of universal hubris that we all seem to be burdened with.

The reality is that every truth we come across is already part of us; at least, we are able to comprehend it on the surface the moment we hear it. Unfortunately, there is a large gap between comprehending something and truly using it. Speaking from experience, I have often come across the idea that simplicity is somehow positive and beautiful in itself. I would nod when I read or heard it, eager to move on to the next thought. This apparently trivial decision to turn my mind away from this claim—that simplicity is powerful—causes many problems down the line.

It is only when life becomes incredibly complex, to the extent that the endless tangle of events seem to strangle you when you close your eyes, that the real power of an idea becomes apparent.[1. That is, if one does not take advantage of meditation, writing and reflection as formal activities.] Just as a computer—which used to work so well—becomes infuriatingly slow as it ages because it has only a limited amount of memory available, so too the human mind becomes intolerably sluggish once too many projects and decisions are ongoing. It is not something to be proud of to have endless half-finished projects: it is a lack of control.

This sluggishness does not just affect the quality of decisions and thus outcomes. It affects one's mood, one's relationships and one's sense of self. What starts as simple overloading of one's capacity ("I've been so busy lately!") quickly becomes a dangerous situation. The calmest disposition plunges into unnecessary aggression; the strongest relationship starts to fray. If the overload is addressed within days, it is a cautionary tale. If it is fixed in weeks, it is a close shave. If it goes on for months, the risk of mental illness, drug abuse, broken relationships and the gnawing feeling that "I am not who I used to be" becomes likely, if not inevitable.

The solution to all of this is simplicity.

*

A life that has one purpose is simple. A day that has one goal is simple. A goal that has one action required to achieve it to simple.

A life that has various interlocking purposes is complex. A day that has multiple goals is complex. A goal that has several actions required to achieve it is complex.

Complexity is not always negative; it is sometimes necessary. Neither is it true that ultimate simplicity is always desirable.[2. I have found that setting 3 goals for one day is an optimum amount.] Aiming towards simplicity is always beneficial, however.

Consider this scenario: for reasons unknown, the fate of the world rests in your hands. You desire a specific end—you wish to save the world and even make it a better place. On a table in front of you there are two pieces of paper. One has a list with forty actions to be taken. The other has three. Both claim to be the way to save the world.

Which do you choose?

Instinctively, you are likely to reach for the simpler list. Why? Because it is more concise. Because it is clearer. Because it is actually possible. I do not think this is for a vague psychological reason: I believe it is underpinned by biological and logical reasons. It is inefficient to choose complexity over simplicity. If it is possible to perform 40 actions correctly, is not highly likely that performing 3 actions would be easier, more pleasant and the better option? It does not take much to move from the desire to simplicity to the beautiful—and profound—thought that I think is the real power of embracing simplicity and using it to make major decisions in life:

If you can narrow down your options to the fewest number, you will be able to give more energy and effort to each of them. In this way, you can apply the greatest power to the smallest action.

If you consider every decision in life you make to be a kind of division, in which your energy, effort and spirit are divided by the number of tasks to be performed, we see that there is a clear reason for choosing simplicity wherever possible: the fewer decisions, actions and commitments you make, the more of you there is to give to each. It is thus not only easier and more pleasant for you to choose simplicity—it is better for the thing you give your time to.

*

The irony of discussing simplicity is that it appears to be simple. It is difficult to focus on something supposedly simple to long. Perhaps that is the reason we find ourselves committed to too many (often worthy) projects and people. Our optimism and love of helping jumps the gun before we assess our ability. Usually, it is possible to achieve a large amount of things for a long period of time. The point is that this places the achievements over the achiever. The work quickly becomes a drain and our passion begins to drain.

Worse, we seem to conflate simplicity with ease. Whilst it can often be the case that simplifying life makes it easier, the reality is that the difficulty of a task is inherent in the task itself. It is easy to perform a workout. It is difficult to chain 300 workouts together without missing a session. Yet simplicity is still a powerful tool. If the workout itself is made simpler—stripped of unnecessary exercises, for example—it makes the more difficult task simpler.

Indeed, simplifying life is not necessarily easy. The initial act of cutting things out is often the most difficult part of organising one's life.[3. This is the real power of simplicity: it highlights what is important, strips away what is not and redistributes that time back to the important task.] Yet once this is complete, the benefits begin rolling in. They do not stop. Instead of absurd time-management techniques ("I'll do this for fifteen minutes, then switch back to that, then I'll go there and carry on, before returning there and maybe doing that along the way"), the tasks themselves take priority: "I will do this." Describing your day, or the actions required to achieve your task, is usually the best measurement of how complex or simple it is.

Simplicity, then, is not the same thing as easiness. Yet simplicity does make life easier once the initial configuration is completed. If you see this configuration as the funeral of complexity, then you have an accurate picture: even in death, complexity is an awful drain on the human spirit. Simplicity, however, is light, free and clear. It makes your purpose of life clear, and takes the guesswork out of decisions so that you can focus on what matters.

*

title: La Retraite (Or, The Retreat) (short story)
content:
La Retraite


By Luke Labern


I


He stepped off the train and pulled his cap forward, so as to shade his eyes.

His worn boots made a slight tap as he walked across the large, sun-dried paving stones of the platform, though the noise was subsumed into the general hum of the people present. The train itself was still whistling slightly, as steam continued to rise into the air above the black locomotive, blending into the heat above. It was an exceptionally hot day; he took off his denim jacket and laid it across his right shoulder, the fingers of his right hand forming a hook.

He cut through the assorted people and made a distinctive figure: he was paler than they were, taller than they were, more isolated than they were. He stood around six-one, a lean figure. What little of him could be seen revealed a taut musculature; he had thin forearms, but the veins crisscrossing hinted at his strength. His upper arms were slightly bigger, but what stood out was the tone of his muscles. No one paid much attention to him, however; they were focused on the departures and the arrivals of their loved ones. Without saying a word, he left the station and followed a dirt track, the dust clinging to his boots and blending in with the chocolate brown of his corduroy trousers.

He kept to the side of the track, often stepping on the grass hanging over the edge where the field met the dried mud—which, after he took his next step, raised slightly, each blade sitting a little, before falling once again, accepting its new position. His white t-shirt gradually became saturated with sweat; the middle of his wet back held the material in place whilst the lower portions blew gently in the slight wind.

The landscape was flat and open: only the track had any sense of direction. The grass was a particularly brilliant shade of green, the sun now hanging high, feeding it. There were only two clouds in the sky: a huge cumulonimbus inching across so slowly as to appear motionless. Only he seemed to move.

He continued to follow the track, pausing only to readjust the shoulder on which his jacket rested. The sun crawled across the sky; the cloud moved into the distance and the landscape revealed more of itself. More of the same.

Eventually, a little brown dot in the distance revealed itself as a farmhouse.

Approaching the property, he heard a gentle, rhythmic thwack. As he neared the front of the farmhouse, which possessed its own little track to distinguish it form the larger track upon which he had travelled, he spotted the form of someone laying an axe into a tree trunk. The form was blocked off by one of the posts that held the front of the farmhouse’s roof over the porch. He caught a glimpse of long blonde hair following the motion of its owner as the form picked up another block of wood to be chopped.

He stopped for the first time to study the property, finding it small and modest. He approached the front of the property and saw a name engraved on the front: ‘Béringer’.

He knocked on the front door.

No one answered.

He paused, considering what to do—but he made no move towards the girl chopping wood, who had not heard his gentle knock. He tried again, and this time heard movement: the sound of feet shuffling accompanied by a knock from inside.

An old man opened the door. ‘Oui?’

‘Do you own this farm?’ The younger man spoke in French.

‘Oui.’ The old man leant desperately on a crude walking stick; he was out of breath. He wore dungarees despite the heat.

‘Are you M. Bérginer?’

M. Béringer nodded, so as to break the monotony of his replies.

The young man asked him, in as few words as possible, if he could lodge at the farm in exchange for work.

As he was in the process of asking this, the wood-chopper stepped onto the porch to her father’s left and asked who the man was in a polite way, though also assessing the nature of the man’s visit. She took her father’s arm.

The man looked at the girl’s face very quickly and noted only that she was exceedingly pretty, possessing a pair of deep blue eyes that perfectly offset her pink lips, before returning his focus to the old man.

The man repeated as much as was necessary, and finished his question.

‘Come inside,’ said M. Béringer.

‘Sit, father,’ said the girl, leading the way inside. The old man acquiesced, slowly and awkwardly lowering himself into a dark green armchair.

‘Would you like anything?’ the girl asked.

‘Non, merci.’ The man took his cap off, exposing a handsome, clean-shaven face. His cheeks were thin, and his chin long—he had a distinctive look, but it was the sort of look one remembered fondly. His skin was a healthy brown, though nothing compared to his hosts’; they lived in the sun. He was merely a visitor. He had short brown hair, as dark as it could have been whilst still remaining brown. The sweat that had accumulated under his cap left his hair sticking to his forehead; he slicked his hair back. His hosts were not put off by this, being used to sweating themselves. Though his good looks were hard to ignore, there was something about him that made it difficult to look away.

The girl was attempting to decipher this very point as she stood to her father’s side, her hands resting in front of her, holding one another. She unconsciously squeezed her left thumb with her right hand, which she always did when lost in thought.

The visitor again raised the question.

‘We do not have much here; only a mattress in a spare room.’

‘That is all I ask,’ he replied. ‘I do not ask for luxury.’

The girl continued to scrutinise his face. She noted his small nose, his almost feminine features, his grey eyes. These she found intriguing in isolation, but together they created a unique composition. When the man looked away from her father to her, she quickly looked away. It was obvious that she had been staring at him.

‘May I ask why you have come here? We are very out of the way.’ M. Béringer again coughed; the girl placed her hand on his shoulder.

‘I came only to work.’

‘We cannot pay you.’

‘I do not ask for payment; I just want to work.’

The girl continued to stare at him. This handsome man, who looked slightly awkward, hunched in an armchair sitting to the right of the father, was too tall for the farmhouse: both the father and his daughter were short—the father around ten inches shorter than the man, the girl at least a foot. But it was not this that drew her attention. It was his eyes. Or, rather, their setting.

The man had many wrinkles—an unusually large amount of deep, prominent emotion. He was almost emotionless at the present moment, but his face told the story of a deeply expressive man. The lighting in the farmhouse was not particularly bright, but she could see that little flecks of dirt had set themselves into the man’s face. There were two distinctive lines drawn into forehead, which, though subtle, became quite apparent when he spoke. Around his eyes, however, there were many more: if one were to consider only his eyes, one would have thought him to have existed for fifty years. His eyes looked as though they had seen many things.

‘We are only a small farm,’ the old man continued; ‘we subsist on what we produce. I am too old; my daughter is forced to do the work.’ The old man smiled sadly. ‘If you can help her, you can stay with us for as long as you like.’

‘Merci.’

‘Sophie, please take our guest—I am sorry; I forgot to ask your name.’

‘Isaac,’ he replied.

‘Sophie, please take Isaac to the spare room.’

She blushed upon hearing her name; she had been considering Isaac—contemplating him. She nodded, quickly turning her head so as too hide her blushed cheeks. ‘This way.’

The farm house was small; it took them only a matter of seconds to reach the other end of the building, through a narrow corridor and into small room with a dressing table and, as described, a small, thin mattress on the floor.

Sophie led him into the middle of the room and turned around, not realising that he was standing right behind her. They found themselves face to face in this cramped room—the brightest in the house, for the window took up most of the width of the wall.

She felt a shiver run through her, quickly followed by a rising feeling of warmth. She found herself looking up at his face, once again looking at his eyes.

He recognised the nature of the encounter immediately and stepped back, but not before instinctively studying her.

Her hair was golden, though a particularly light shade in this light. She had a small face, which was exceedingly pretty: her eyebrows were thin, though her lips were not. Her hair was pinned behind her left ear, which for some reason caught his attention. Her small ear, and the new angle of her face this exposed, led him to pause and study her a second longer than he would have liked. He could see no blemish on her face at all, and her dark blue eyes seemed to penetrate him. Her youth added an extra layer of attractiveness; where he possessed tired wrinkles, she had only taut, untroubled skin.

He felt the same warmth rising up in him.

‘May I shower?’ he asked, seeking a reason to leave her.

‘Y-yes,’ she stuttered, once again feeling her cheeks go hot. ‘Outside.’

II


A second axe was found, and Isaac made it his own.

The ferocity and focus with which he tore through work was something to behold. At first, the two of them took it in turns to chop; hers, a skilful action which used as little energy as possible—his, all power. Her arms were well toned; she had been chopping wood since she was a little girl. She was sixteen now, and had the healthy body of one who lived on hard physical labour and high quality food, cultivated by herself. Perhaps equally importantly, she possessed the glow and confidence of autonomy. She was entirely responsible for her continued existence. Her calm and effective approach to chopping mirrored this: she took each action as the constituent part of a larger project, expending precisely the amount of energy required. Her thoughts were focused not only on the task at hand, but on the bigger picture: the work yet to be done. She was able to chop without breaking a sweat.

He, on the other hand, attacked the job. His swings were violent and reckless. More than a few times he came close to injuring himself, at which Sophie let out a small shriek. She attempted to teach him advanced techniques, but it quickly became apparent that his work was for him a form of catharsis.  He let out barely audible grunts as he made his way through each piece of wood, creating such large arcs with his swing that the sweat he quickly accrued flew in a semi-circle, the droplets illuminated by the sunlight from above. In the background all that could be seen were the endless fields of grass, the dirt track and the perfectly still sky.

Much of the time, Sophie stayed with him. They quickly became easy with one another, neither of them alluding to their first meeting alone—that aspect of their relationship was addressed solely through their eyes. At times, however, Isaac became so consumed by his physical labour that he seemed almost possessed: he would chop one piece of wood and, in the same motion, would reach for the next piece, before attacking that without pause. This was not done fluidly, however. It was done aggressively, and thus awkwardly: it was at these times that it seemed likely that he would swing so wildly as to miss the stump altogether and split his lower leg in half.

Sophie left him at these moments solely because she did not want to see him hurt himself—she did, however, stay within earshot.

After the wood had been chopped, they then tended to the chickens. Sophie was pleased more by companionship than by the division of labour—though that allowed her the time to study this reticent man. She attempted to ask natural questions, phrasing them politely, but Isaac seemed only to want to discuss the work.

‘How long have you been in the region?’ she asked, noticing one of the hens hobbling and tending to it.

‘Not long,’ he replied. ‘What is wrong with her?’

‘Her foot.’ Sophie picked up the hen, which was flapping wildly, and exposed a cut.

‘What’s the procedure?’ he asked matter-of-factly. He spoke seriously, though Sophie was calm.

‘I’ll just keep an eye on her; if she doesn’t improve, we’ll have her for dinner.’

Isaac nodded solemnly.

As they made their way through the various jobs to be undertaken, a pattern emerged. Sophie would attempt to start conversation, but Isaac would dictate the direction: always about the work. He also carried his axe around with him.

‘Why do you carry that axe with you?’

‘I may need it,’ he said, smiling. The lines on his face became striking; Sophie could not help but look, fascinated.

Sophie laughed sweetly. ‘We could share the axe, you know.’

Isaac looked at her in reply, his smile having faded. A feeling of warmth rose up between them once again; he quickly moved on to the next job.

At dinner, the three of them sat around a small table and ate from the produce they had farmed. Sophie served her father.

‘How did you get on?’ the old man asked, in a tone different from that he had used in the beginning.

‘It was excellent,’ Isaac replied. ‘You have a beautiful farm.’

Sophie impulsively looked at him, hearing the word ‘beautiful.’

‘Thank you, Isaac,’ said the old man, taking a mouthful of chicken. ‘I hear you’ve been working very hard.’

Sophie blushed.

‘I hope so; I am certainly clumsy. But I enjoy farming very much.’

The dinner continued, largely in silence: Sophie spoke only to her father. She was tired of trying to engage Isaac in conversation—or, more accurately, she felt too fragile to be ignored once again. She was glad to let her father try; Isaac—perhaps out of respect—replied to all of his questions, though this was likely because they largely concerned practical matters. Isaac seemed very eager to learn the technical side of farming, and agricultural economics.

After dinner, the old man drank wine. Isaac declined, as did Sophie. Isaac took his leave early, and headed to his room after thanking his hosts.

‘Well, what do you think, Sophie? Is he a help?’ The old man’s tone was completely different. The last vestige of formality had been shed.

‘I think he is a great help…’

‘But?’

‘But nothing. He is very able, although he is emotional in his work, rather than practical.’ She paused, thinking about Isaac being in his room—and the time she shared with him there. ‘I enjoy the extra company. It’s been a very long time since there have been three of us here.’

‘I am glad. Although I must say I have missed you today, it is nice to have an extra pair of hands. He’s not very talkative, though, is he?’

Sophie did not reply.

‘We’ll see,’ the old man said, coughing. ‘Now, will you read for me?’

‘Of course, father,’ Sophie said, heading to the bookshelf in order to engage in their traditional reading session. ‘What would you like to read today?’

‘You know my favourite.’

III


The days continued to pass.

The work remained the same; Isaac remained a passionate, rather than pragmatic, worker. He seemed to prefer the physical labour much more than the delicate work; Sophie was quick to notice this and allotted him those jobs which allowed him to expend the energy he seemed driven to use. She continued to attempt to probe him, restoring her energy at night—laying awake for several hours each night, thinking of how odd life was, how it changed without warning; how she could never have predicted her current circumstances; how he literally appeared one day, and changed the structure of her domestic—and emotional—life). Over time, he began to open up emotionally. He responded to her light comments with jokes of his own; he came to know the various animals and they gave them names. Their camaraderie was the primary feature of their relationship: each learned from the other, and they saw one another as peers, rather than strangers.

M. Béringer spent his time inside, though he exerted as much energy as he could to bring himself to the window to watch the interaction of his daughter with their visitor. He perceived well that she was studying Isaac; he could not take his eyes off her own. He was indeed interested in Isaac and his unique approach to work, but his attention always centred upon his daughter. If this young man was not present, he would have been outside with her—or, at least, expecting her regular visit inside. With the visitor, however, he knew that she had a new outlet. He welcomed it. Though he was largely pleased at the experience for her sake, being unable to smile himself when he saw the two of them joking, he felt troubled by the fact Sophie had foregone many social encounters like this for his sake. Isaac’s presence was for him bittersweet—largely because it highlighted his own flaws.

Whilst the two of them spent much of their time jesting, Isaac remained prone to moments of brooding intensity—he would cut short a peal of laughter and clench his jaws as if holding something back. Sophie, at these moments, would let her laughter fade gently. She wondered what was behind the changes in his emotion; wondered why she was not able to fully heal or distract him.

At dinner, too, Isaac began to open up. He and M. Béringer discussed literature and philosophy. Isaac, quite enigmatically, would quote—thus starting conversation—and the old man would give his often curt opinion, at which the three of them would begin laughing. Sophie would watch and listen, for the most part: for her, these matters were not interesting. Isaac was interesting. Who was he, and why was he there?

‘I don’t know where you’ve come from, Isaac—and I know you won’t answer my questions—but I find your love for labour quite fascinating,’ the old man would say. Isaac stayed with them after dinner; as the old man drank wine, he would become quite open. Though Isaac abstained, he opened up too—as if relying on the fact that the old man would remember little of what he said.

Sophie noted that during the day, he would focus his attention on her, whilst at night he would focus on her father. She wondered when he focused on himself.

‘My friend, I love it here. I adore the simplicity of the work. There are no complications: the goals are very simple. You need shelter, you need food: so you work each day to achieve that. You go to sleep each night having achieved that, and you are so tired that you sleep soundly. You wake up the next day and carry on. You are… accompanied by your family, and you face no financial problems. What money you do need you get from selling wood, of which there is an abundance. I can think of very little that I would rather do than live like this until the day I die.’ Isaac became quite passionate; his face revealed pure joy. The lines in his face that revealed themselves only when he smiled became prominent.

‘Although I no longer work—for I am near the end (don’t worry, Sophie!)—I do understand your thinking. I am very tired; it is difficult for me to do the few things I can do. I do, however, remember vividly my working days. I remember growing up a boy, and living in a place very similar to this. My friends were always the animals around me. I mourned their deaths: but I respected them as much as the people I knew. For, though they could not speak, they were the ones who could speak to me through their presence alone. We did not need words.’

Sophie looked at Isaac, and caught him looking at her. For the first time, he did not look away. He continued to look at her, aware that the old man was quite inebriated. He was, however, listening very carefully to his words.

Sophie, with her heart beating rapidly and the palms of her hands moist with sweat, felt her chest heave as they looked at one another.

‘I believe that how one lives says much more about them than what they say. I know you are from England, Isaac: I think people there do more talking than they do acting. We are simple people, but we are happy people.’

‘I couldn’t agree more,’ Isaac said, simply. ‘What I love most about your way of life is what Rousseau would have respected: you are very close to nature, in many respects. I do not think you believe you own this land; you simply cultivate it. I see no intrusion of the state, nor reliance upon it. I see a man and his daughter. I see love, I see respect and I see life. You do not worry about the things I worry about where I come from. And that… makes me love you.’ He clenched his jaws at this revealing phrase. He immediately looked embarrassed, but the old man reached across the table and held Isaac’s hand, squeezing it.

Isaac looked up at him and saw the old man’s simple, smiling face. Neither said a word. He looked at Sophie, who looked surprised—her father, although a kind man, did not display emotion like this. She felt herself well up; as did Isaac.

‘Thank you,’ Isaac whispered, taking his leave.

As emotions once again rose, Isaac left: Sophie realised that this was his reaction to all forms of intensity. His departure did indeed reduce the tension, but it also left a hole where he had been. The father and daughter sat together for a little while, both now reflecting on how life had thrown Isaac their way.

‘Shall I read, father?’ she asked, after a short while.

‘Yes,’ her father replied, wiping something from his eye. ‘Rousseau. A Discourse.’

IV


 The next morning, Sophie brought Isaac a glass of fresh milk and a thick slice of bread for breakfast. She knocked, but heard no reply.

Opening the door, she found he was gone. All that remained was a piece of paper, folded in half and laid on the pillow.

Sophie knew instantly what had happened—although she did not understand why—and felt her hands tremble. She placed the tray she was holding on the floor and picked up the note, which read:

            Thank you for having me.

V


 Isaac stepped onto the train and pulled his cap forward, so as to hide his identity from those who might knew him.

On the train, a solemn-looking woman dressed in a dark blue suit dress handed him a script.

‘You have twenty-four hours to learn your lines. We’ll be in London by tonight.’

title: The Human Condition (poem)
content:
Quantify success, for I calculate
That any answer has no telling trait.
One man's hell can be another's lover --
So show me one who will thus discover

Any universal and agreed stick
To measure joy that is not a vain trick.
The doubt which follows leads many astray,
And though I wish for nothing but to stay.

Past success cannot sustain happiness --
But tragedy follows any excess:
Where lies the balance, where sits perfection?
If I'm right, in introspection.

To accept one's flaws is a kind blessing
But one which requires a life of stressing.
We did not sign up, but we choose
To continue -- no one wishes to lose

This chance to breathe, exist and empathise --
Regardless of the times we despise.
As life goes on, so does evolution --
The human condition: no solution.

title: To England in Spring (sonnet)
content:
The skies alive with ecstasy and light --
Emotion reigns and rings with summer's tint.
The sun in bloom, the season strong and bright:
A look above leads one to smile and squint.
And thus this love of life swells to blooming
Aligned to nature's growth. As old persona
Shatters, the darkness which was once a-looming
Assumes the face of grace known as Verona:
Escaping England -- Summer's surest gift!
I question why, when clouds reveal their pearl:
The beauty present could no English shift
From here, as spring, indeed, does thus unfurl.
The land itself recites the national song;
Throughout it all, I feel that I belong.

title: Combustion Triangle (poem)
content:
Sorrow, anger, self-belief
Mortal ties with no relief.
Fight the way, resist the numb
Suffer, for the night will come.
Dusk permits suspension of talk --
Follow still the thoughts that stalk.
Times of wrenched smiles lack the jolt
Brought by life. Appended bolt
Lies for sake of grace desired:
Skills no poet once admired.

Fighting labels to be free
Taken from the bourgeoisie:
Fitting in or standing out?
Questions soothe the once devout --
Media lies may trick most;
Answers quickly lead to boast --
Boasting gives to sore regret...
Never let them crimes forget.
Shuffled pride can well provide
Doubts -- but don't you dare reside.

This is not the master plan --
Just a flame that I can fan.

title: Flow (essay)
content:
Optimism is, of course, defined by what we would like to happen. The substance of our dreams, those images and events that provide a special sort of psychological pleasure which nevertheless spreads throughout the body and can even get the tiniest hairs on our bodies standing on end, are composed almost wholly of positive proposals for the future. Naturally, there is good reason for this fact: why would anyone dream of a future in which they were beset by the sort of problems they are experiencing now (lack of money, strains in their personal relationships, a bout of depression, insomnia, and so on)? This is, after all, a human being's personal utopia. I have long argued that this insistence on dreaming—that is, that one should purposely cultivate their dream and spend each day trying to further their success in this area. I stand by what I've said, though due to events in my life that I believe have matured me several years in only the space of one, I would like to add what I consider a unique component of the lifestyle of the dreamer who eventually succeeds.

I call this concept "flow".

I do claim that flow "exists"; it is the description of what I consider to be an attitude, or a powerful way of thinking that we all deploy at various at times. However, because the concept has not been thoroughly explored (I, certainly, have not heard anything on the topic apart from the saying "go with the flow"), I think that a large swathe of perfectly intelligent people are missing out on something that could help them in life. To reiterate: this is not the postulation of some new life-force. It is an attempt to hold on to, and to expand on, something that you have experienced at several times in life (possibly several times a year). Like "luck", it is not something which exists in and of itself, but is a powerful conceptual tool that can allow us to make peace with the world, our place in it, and—most importantly—can aid us in achieving our dreams.

Without


Whereas my focus on dreaming and on optimism is very much a pro-active philosophy, the concept of flow is essentially a psychological (and to some extent, philosophically grounded) tool which essentially dampens pessimism. It is in a powerful sense a form of damage limitation. I am well aware that this quite unlike anything I have written about before. That is precisely because I had not been exposed to certain forms of damage—or, rather, I had not dealt with them adequately. I have, like you, been crushed by various in events. Despite the obvious fact that our many failings are far more similar than our successes, we still focus on success: in the time and place in which we live, we are defined largely by how successful we are. Usually, this is measured in things like wealth and status, though I prefer to measure success by how authentic a person is; how free that person is; how that person spends their life. As Bob Dylan said, "a man is a success if he gets up in the morning and gets to bed at night, and in between he does what he wants to do." There are, obviously, more components to success, but I feel that this perhaps the bed-rock. Certainly, it is how I measure myself.

Yet, for all this talk of success, we are forgetting one crucial element: that for every achievement there are innumerable failures. The word "failure" is weighed down by various connotations; I know that I would have winced at writing about failure only months ago. At one's first attempt, it can feel extremely unpleasant to have that word consciously presented to one. I have tended to dissociate "I" and "failure" wherever possible in my life. This has led to much success, but also much anxiety. Vitally, that anxiety has led to more failure. At certain points in my life, I have quite simply wound myself up to an impossible point. With absolutely no physical or external pressures, I have psychologically paralysed myself and failed tasks that, in comparison with the greatest things I have done, are almost embarrassingly easy.

This state of affairs—self-imposed anxiety—is, I believe, extremely common. I have yet to see someone afflicted with anxiety issues speak sense; myself included. It is only when the apparent danger, or stimuli, is long in the past, that common sense has once again returned to analyse what exactly happened. The great tragedy here is that many key events in our lives are in some sense constrained by time: only at certain moments can they be achieved. Exams are a perfect example of this. A brilliant student may be perfectly capable of sweeping away the challenge of an exam, and achieving the highest grade: indeed, they would be able to score highly on perhaps any given day. Any day, that is, except the day of the exam. Yes: it is in that setting of the deadline, that brings along with the seal of finality, that the anxiety begins. The same student who could, if the exam was sprung at random, quite easily ace it—is completely overwhelmed by the build-up. The days tick down. Two weeks. One week. Five days. Two days. Tomorrow. Twelve hours. Two hours. Five minutes.

A never ending drip, where each second sees the heart beat faster, the nerves shriek just a little higher, and the student just that little bit less able to perform to the true extent of their capabilities.

The exam begins. The exam is simple: the work has been done; the knowledge is there; this is a formality. Yet something is different. That anxiety is no longer a subtle swirling in the stomach: it is some sort of syndrome. It takes over the mind and the body, and renders simple tasks almost impossible. The clock ticking becomes quite literally a measure of death. What at first appeared to be ample time, is now nowhere near enough. Various bodily functions become inverted, and the wrong things take priority. This is a time for the mind to take over—yet the body is wailing.

These states of affairs continue—until the exam is over, and all returns to how it should have been. Only, that was quite literally a storm—and this is quite literally devastation. Not only has the exam gone incorrectly, but the hard work that had been undeniably done has been cast in a new light. It was, in a sense, all for nothing. There has been no justice here. Dreams have not been achieved: life has gone wrong.

This simple example is only one of what I believe is a family of errors that can be avoided. Whereas without the concept of flow (or rather, the suitable application of it) one is quite likely to peak the wrong time and be exhausted when the time for action comes, with flow, one is much more able to give things their appropriate time and energy. Truly, there is nothing worse than giving 100% to an activity that requires only 20%—and finding oneself able to give only 20% to that which requires far, far more.

Flow


Water

title: Art Through Science (essay)
content:
If science is the best way of knowing the world without, art is the best way of knowing the world within.[1. To be specific, I mean the lived experience: what it feels like to be a human.]

The tension between art and science is patently false. It makes no more sense to be either a scientist or an artist than it does to be either a film-lover or a music-lover. They are different subjects, but both stem from the same root. The root that science and art share is a love of wisdom. How that wisdom is earned—through painstaking research and experimentation, standing on the shoulders of giants, the shimmering of a guitar string, simply translating private experience or through the perfect placement of a phrase on the page—does not matter. The relationship between science and art is not only beneficial to both, but it is infinitely better for any individual to hone their skills and knowledge of each than it is to give up on either as "something other people do".

All attempts to divide human knowledge should be resisted fiercely and with as much intensity as possible. Anyone who claims that a certain type of knowledge is not for you should be escorted from the building or assassinated; whichever is most effective. All human knowledge and all human achievement is the birthright of every human being, regardless of intelligence, experience, race, religion, etc. Whilst it may seem harmless—because trivial—anyone who claims that only certain types of people can partake in their domain is as close to evil as it is possible to be.

Just as it is important to know the basics of biology and physics so that one better appreciate the world around them, knowledge of Shakespeare's works is a limitless source of power when one comes to reflect on the human condition or the struggles one currently faces. In science one finds objectivity; in art one finds meaning. Mine is a statement of utter clarity: any individual who neglects either science or art is half a human. This goes for those who have no interest in pursuing either as a career as it does for those who are. A human is a human, and any human will benefit from the sublime heights of all human endeavour.

The purpose of this essay is to examine a specific example of how an appreciation of science[2. Specifically, the scientific method as a means to separate logic from emotion in order to achieve one's goals.] can produce finer, more authentic and more meaningful art.[3. I believe this carries over to almost anything one could hope to do. For example, the use of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for a range of mental illnesses works primarily because it turns the subject into a scientist interested in their own cognitive behaviour. The same thing that works here, in the darkest of times, is equally valuable when trying to reach new heights.]

The Scientific Method

The Artist as Scientist

Conclusion

title: Resume (poem)
content:
For I was once a saddened man
Whose passion struck him down
And though the world did cry for him
He could not find renown.

That time has come and gone again
Like light above the earth;
And though it was a lasting pain
He found again his worth.

Cerebral channels didn’t move;
Coagulated thoughts
And though his mind was whirring full
He had too strong retorts.

The puzzles asked for retraced steps
And silence thus was caused —
And through considered mental reps
Resume from where he paused.

title: Dichotomy (poem)
content:
I need protection from impurity.
From dust of doubt which seeps through aplomb:
A truer version, no society;
Internal combustion, a thinking bomb.

A dualism, a contrast – we juxtapose
Like A to B, like black to white, like this
To that – a lie which we try to expose
Where consciousness, where sense, it goes amiss.

A deeper tunnel, path of unknown length:
Incomprehensible. Where no ego
Is egoism in its strongest strength
Where what’s above is the same as below.

How long it lasts is a matter of luck
And meditation philosophical.
An oily grip on the best things to pluck:
For me, the abstract is the topical.

For grey does not exist in my design;
Just back and white through which I opine.

title: The Pink Russian (poem)
content:
180° one

A cause not caused, for I create:
And you — you wear your own attire —
We play our roles on every day
We do our best till we retire —

Bow out — we all have influence.
We fluctuate in right, in wrong;
In love, and hate, in consequence:
A fact: we are not here too long.

There’s but one life, there is no other
But even if there were a choice
Would you replace your own mother
Or throw away your being’s voice?

A life with scars, with pain, and profit —
Would you embrace death and face black
Whole nothingness? Time to cough it.
Or shall we take a few steps back?

180° two

Grip your conscience by the face;
Eye-to-eye, you question it:
“Who am I? Where do I place
All my time — Where do I fit?”

Ask these things, find your true way;
Seconds pass, but which to chase?
Do we live in the night, or day?
Much to do and much to trace —

Woke one day and all was well:
Woke the next and felt like death.
On which of these should I now dwell?
Of which to use, or save my breath?

Most our life we’re not ourselves:
Briefly, though, we all connect.
In these moments there are no shelves
We open up — and we reflect.

title: On Procrastination (poem)
content:
When allocating time
   To master any art
Is it a crime to pause one’s strength
   To extradite their heart?

*

This poem was originally posted on my Tumblr.

title: Bark/Bite (poem)
content:
(Bark)
The people say I’m cryptic; odd –
  Off-kilter; dark –
And in my mind and in my thought
  Rough like underlying bark.

Thus hidden away – absolute.
  It’s all because of hate –
Or passion – when men over step;
  Tempt me to twist their fate.

Possession? No – relationship.
  So why the need to interfere?
A missing hand the prize
  If you grab what I hold dear.

Aren’t teeth in place to tear?
  Aren’t men alive to live?
Is hate not fuelled by care?
  How much am I to bare?

(Bite)

We flex – our muscles or our mind –
  I just contract them both.
Where nothing’s left to chance
  Let that be quoth.

When I am dead, no more a man
  Let it be said
That I stayed true to this
  When this is read.

Autobiography
  Or abstract – ‘tis all the same:
I breathe in different ways
  And always knew my name.

A label aiding me –
  To help us all discern;
A man who stood to part the sea –
  My name – Labern.

title: The Philosophy of Love (poem)
content:
Poetry: the philosophy of love –
  With fluid promises it teases us,
It divides and contains like a glove
  Holds fingers – unbound yet united – thus
A form through which the paradoxes reign
  A place where I find solidarity
Where otherwise such chaos is called bane;
  Where otherwise too difficult to be.
In changing times where hands clutch less at pens
  And more at throats and electricity
Those universals: the whos, the whys and whens –
  A pure, philosophical clarity.
A draught of pretence or a fatalism
An aesthetic anaesthetic – truism.

title: Sonnet to My Lover (poem)
content:
Through day and night, the sun and moon delight
  In casting and revolving, marking time –
Yet since I first beheld your form, I might
  Forget the light, the dark and set to rhyme:
A beauty truly staggering and pure
  Of such vehemence that whilst instinct cries
To eat, and drink, and sleep – my lover’s lure
  Ensnares and draws me in – the bluest eyes –
The softest lips and most enchanting skin;
  A breath and expression second to none
Whose presence and charm I’m eternally in;
  Yet time has no meaning – all said and done:
When parted, I am lost in an abstract –
Only on seeing your face do I feel intact.

title: Signature (poem)
content:
I
Swagger – stamping signature:
Stun the world with ligature
Pouncing, seizing every day
Self-rhythms the only way –
Off-beat, on-beat, all the same
Glory yours, so too the blame –
Wear only you and your name.

II
Stumble, simmer – simply boil
Don’t regret, for all your toil,
Filled with brutal mediocrity
Now has bloomed, it’s clear to see:
Success, success – a fail – pause;
Don’t forget, you are the cause –
Swipe – and then retract those claws.

III
Swagger – stamping signature
Such subtle implicature –
What an air to bring with you:
Odd to them, your point of view –
All you know – breathe different air –
Linger in their confused stare,
Walk right past what isn’t fair.

IV
Silently await the hour
Mood ebbing low, debase, sour –
Thunder strikes and thoughts erupt
Eye-to-eye with those corrupt,
Don’t say a word – just be sure
What you say – how you live – pure:
Stamp your swagger’s signature.

title: Twisting Clichés (poem)
content:
I lately had
  A waivering heart
Now my blood pumps
  To the wrong part

But when did I
  Let doubt destroy
The very things
  That make me royal

Make me a king –
  When in my mind
No pleasure pars
  With that I find

When I sit down,
  Set sail to cares
And watch my pen
  As life ensnares
Me in its grip:
  He who writes, dares.

title: On the Shoulders of Giants (poem)
content:
With leaps and bounds achieved before my birth
 One wonders where history will have time
To cement my being’s importance to Earth
 In my great passion – in language and rhyme
Such things a man will retain rigor mortis
Explains my attachment to English – this.

Yet on the shoulders of giants I stand
 And only allowed to touch such great heights
By the passion of flames they have fan’d –
 A story of must haves – not of I mights:
You heroes inspire – in life and death –
Bestowing me with thoughts, music and breath.

title: Reel (poem)
content:
Determinism puncturing the night
&nbsp ;Where doubts are juxtaposed with strongest will;
A contradiction resting in the slight
  With my acts the meal and my mind the bill.

A future affliction which touches us
  Now, without remorse in its fateful way
With hidden answers in its asking thus:
   Can you accept the burden, come what may?

A trust in ‘I’ and of reality,
