title: Alcohol and Infidelity (short story)
content:
Good looking, yes. What else? Problematic. Attention-seeking. Narcissistic. Selfish. Apparently, she was also irre-fucking-sistible. I’m an idiot. Even recalling it, I want to slash my wrists and dive headfirst through a window, immolate myself and scream until I cough up blood. There really isn’t anything I can look back on with more spite, with more fury, with more regret than this. My blood is boiling just entertaining these thoughts: I will have to be very particular with what I say. I won’t recall how we got together, or why (I don’t think there is a why which is half the problem): rather, I’ll dive right into those moments which lacerated me and left my self-worth pouring out of mental wounds that have now scarred. It’s obvious that it ended, so there’s no point pretending that it’s suspenseful: I eventually found the courage (or intelligence) to end it; only a few months prior to the main narrative, in fact. It was the only relationship I had embarked on since my first one; I took a good year out to savour the sanctity of reflection and making sure I was mentally stable.

And then it took about three days to lose it all.

Picture, if you will, a phone in my hand. It’s three o’ clock in the morning; I’ve just been awoken by a phone call (whose sound now sends shivers down my spine: no wonder I got rid of it). Half-asleep, I’m greeted by the voice of someone very particular. As I listen to her, my mental image is quite clear: blond hair, blue eyes. What else needs to be said about that? I couldn’t get the accurate picture in your head if I tried, so let’s work with that. Drunk, she says ‘I’m so sorry . . . I’ve got something to tell you.’
My heart now racing, palpitating; fearing the worst, I ask, ‘What is it?’

Thorough tears the other end.

‘What is it?’ I repeat.

‘I slept with someone.’

The clock stops ticking. I think my heart stopped beating. Those few seconds where I use my mental cutlery to chop up the linguistic content I’ve just been served, and then dine on each particular syllable, taking it in, then savouring it as a whole . . . those were the last few moments on this planet where I can say I had any wholesome, uninterrupted, positive feelings towards this girl. After that, what? A mixture of hate, self-hate, disdain and confusion.

No one had ever cheated on me before. I had never cheated on anyone. Never will. (And it would take an idiot or a dire waste of oxygen to do so, especially after they’ve been cheated on.)

Infidelity: my curse, my burden, my torturer.

The first and only time a source of depression has ever come externally to me. So why does it feel like I’m being ripped apart from the inside out? Thoughts on fire, I ask banal and meaningless questions:

‘Who? When? . . . Why?’

More tears. More time to wonder about the details. Grimy hands, groping, orgasms. I want to tear someone’s throat out.

Possibly my own.

‘A couple of months ago . . .’

How does that make sense? Why would someone cheat on you and then tell you two months later? I asked her a similar question.

‘I—I was too weak. Too nervous. I needed alcohol in my system.’

The best part was, I’d spent the evening with her before she went out clubbing (for some waste of space’s birthday). What better way to spend an eve than covered in other people’s sweat and your own regret? Apparently none.

Looking for something to say, I keep asking the same questions. ‘Who with?’

She wouldn’t say. ‘Couldn’t’ say – the mark of a liar.

‘Hold on.’ Finally I trace the dates she’s giving me. I almost jump out of bed (where does it matter where I’m sitting or standing, really?): ‘we’ve only be going out for two months . . . What the f—‘

‘I was scared. Scared of falling for you—‘

What a bunch of bullshit.

‘It was . . . two days after we got together.’

Never has a sentence ripped through me with quite such force as that one. Like a bullet, the entry wound was simple and concise: right in the ear. The exit wound, however, was not only brutal to look at – it took me months and months to finally find the fucking bullet and sew up the wound.

Tears start rolling down my face; slowly. Nothing dramatic: there are only a few. But within those few droplets it seems as though the world’s misery has found a home. The clock has stopped ticking. All I can hear is my own lack of breath – my complete breathless shock.

Why? Why all this? If we’d only been together for two months, why not get rid? Well, this perfect example of feminine reasoning had truly sunk her claws in. I could feel them start to tear my flesh as I contemplated pulling them out. In those two months I’d become very involved: I thought it was love. Consider the betrayal: all that time, all of it, she’d been lying to me.
‘Not telling the truth isn’t the same as lying’ is what I heard on the other end of the phone.

I threw mine against the wall.

I think I’ll sit in this position where the news broke for a few hours. I certainly won’t be sleeping. The same soft skin and lips I’d sat and drunk in – well, it was all too late. Someone had already gotten there, said whatever needed to be said to ‘seduce’ (what does that word even mean anymore?) her, and had his way. Three minutes of gritty fucking ecstasy, scraped knees, whimpering sounds, drunken slobbering – and a whole lot of pain for me. All of this had taken place in such a wonderful place. A bed, perhaps? In the lounge of some lothario? No, not quite:

In an alleyway.

*


 All these details came later. All I could get out of her at first was a wonderfully vague story about ‘some guy called Josh’, a ‘tall, dark-haired’ guy who wouldn’t leave her alone. She told him she had a boyfriend but he persisted. Sitting at a table in some club, he eventually leaned in and kissed her: she kissed back. Later, after a few drinks, they found themselves out behind the nightclub having a cigarette. Alone. In the meantime, I was at home probably feeling worldly, philosophising about the mind-body problem – or more realistically, I was wondering how she was doing, what she was up to.

She was too drunk to say no but not drunk enough to make sure he wore a condom. It was ‘forgettable’, or ‘awful’, or whatever the fuck she said – then he walked off and joined his friends whilst she probably lit up a post-coital cigarette.

This is the story I ‘believed’ (though to say I wasn’t sceptical would be a lie) for another year – yes, I stayed with her for a year – until in the final weeks of our relationship when, sitting on a sofa watching some utterly forgettable television programme, the topic randomly flitted through my mind for what must have been the thousandth time.

It turned out her backstory wasn’t even half true. Due to purposeful repression of these events I can’t remember the exact question, but in a matter of seconds I worked out who it was she had had sex with that night: a few seconds later I was standing up almost pulling my hair out; I told her not to come near me but she insisted on trying to hug me as if I was about to leave the planet forever. Luckily, I wasn’t; but that was to be the beginning of the end. My rage got the better of me; a rage that has never been released outside of the sports field or the gym. The results were unpleasant. I messaged the . . . person . . . (of course, she had his number on her phone the whole time – the entire year) and told him what I knew. Obviously, it was quite a while ago: since then he’d had sex with countless numbers of STD-ridden, fake-tan streaked, fake-eyelash dropping girls who dropped their pants before their glass of vodka, so it was probably hard for him to remember which alleyway this was, which blurry human that was on the receiving end of his boy-like frame’s attempt at sexual intercourse.

*


My left hand is around his throat. It’s just he and I in the alleyway; a few weeks after I found out it was he who’d caused all of this. Well, the two of them. Luckily it was a Saturday, so he was out and about, drinking. Not difficult to find. Now he was gasping for air. I can see the sweat run down his arm over the tattoo of his Italian name. He puts both of his hands over mine to try and pull my fingers from the delicate skin on his lightly-stubbled throat which are leaving bruises. I loosen my grip a little before I kill him.

His greasy, short black hair and five-clock shadow make me reflect: I wonder with what passion she kissed him?  I can see the traces of his dimples, the same components of his ‘cheeky chappy’ smile which are distorted with the sobering look of fear that has accosted all of his features. Distress screams out with his features as he struggles for breath.

He’s drunk.

So am I.

I hate alcohol, but I’d been swigging the contents of a square-bottled whiskey jar, neat, all the way here. That’s probably why my grip is so hard: I can’t even hear him squeal. Oh, he just did. It was quite feminine; as if I was dominating him. Oh, I am. I see lipstick at the side of his lips, fading as he continues to sweat.

‘Is that your girlfriend’s?’

He tries to say something but he can’t get the words out. Turns out you need a sufficient opening for your larynx to make words. I take a heart gulp of the whiskey from the bottle in my right hand. It’s about two-thirds of the way finished, so I throw the bottle away and wipe away some of the whiskey which is carelessly trickling down through my beard, which is extremely thick and bedraggled. I’m sweating too, and parts of the fringe from my rather long mid-length hair are sticking to my face. I loosened my grip after repeating my question: I reduced the pressure on his jugular whilst maintaining a thorough and dominating grip around his neck as a whole, to let him know who was in control.

‘Yes,’ he fairly whispered out.

‘Should I go and see her?’ Too menacingly for me. Purely for effect. I couldn’t give a fuck about his girlfriend. She has it bad enough: she thought being with this scumbag would be a good decision. Why would I cause someone like that any further harm? She was doomed already. This isn’t me. But I’m too far in now.

‘Do you know who I am?’

‘No, I don’t – you freak!’

‘Didn’t you get my messages?’ I don’t know how I managed to speak this coolly or clearly.

The flicker of recognition in his eyes: finally, the drunken idiot had put it all together. I could have sworn I felt his body shiver with fear.

‘Well, I said I’d make you pay. You might think you can have sex with whoever the fuck you like . . . but sooner or later someone was going to punish you for complete disregard for everything and everyone other than your own libido.’ He didn’t know what libido meant. ‘Dick. Your dick. You think with your dick.’

Suddenly he had a wave of courage. ‘I know people. I’m out with them right now. Let go of me.’ I obviously wasn’t gripping him hard enough. I pinned his left hand to the wall with my right, dragging his knuckles along the brickwork. I could see from his wincing that it was the right thing to do. He wasn’t striking me with his free hand: if he was, I would have broken it. Somehow, I think he knew that. He knew that I was extremely worked up, if not deranged. Passionate, if not vicious. But I was on the edge between these small inklings of punishment and far more serious one.

‘There’s a reason no one has ever started a fight with me.’ I pulled his cheeks together so his lips were puffed up. He was completely under my control. I could do whatever I wanted. ‘It’s unfortunate that you chose her of all people to sleep with –‘

No, no, that’s not right.

‘”Fuck”, isn’t it? You fucked her. Right?’

No response.

‘That sounds about right. She said it was awful. Not that I care.’ That was a lie. A needless lie. ‘I’m not a killer. I’m not even violent. The funny thing is, I’m a pacifist. But look at me. I’m drunk. I hate drinking. I’ve got some waste of skin pinned to a wall. Look at you! What are you doing with your life? Fucking other people’s girlfriends?’

‘Everyone makes mistakes.’

How true. ‘I’m making a mistake right now.’

‘She treated you like a mug, mate. You should be angry at her, not me,’ he said, trying to loosen my grip – which I duly tightened. On and off. To give him the feeling of being free and then to take it away again.

He was right. What was I doing? I was intoxicated enough to do all this and go against everything I believe in but I wasn’t intoxicated enough to do something I’d really regret. In fact, I wouldn’t regret this at all.

‘If you ever speak my name, think about me, talk about me, tell anyone this happened . . .’

‘I won’t. Just let go of me.’

‘I’m glad you didn’t go for the tough-guy act you seemed to try over the phone. I didn’t believe you. And even if you were a tough guy, what would that matter? Size doesn’t matter. All that matters is passion. Whoever wants to win a fight most, wins. End of. And you have everything to lose. I have nothing left to lose.’ Images flashed back into my head of everything: all the shit I’d put up with for the past year, my own stupidity and weakness, the doubt that had crept into me, the fact I’d chosen such an awful ‘partner’ in the first place. All of this, this wasn’t anger at him: it was anger at me. It was self-destruction through the means of pinning some unintelligent ‘lad’ against a wall and making him fear for his life. I was done with it.

‘Get out of here. Try not to fuck anyone else tonight. Or someone might actually be angry enough to go through with it.’ I released my hand from his throat, which was now thoroughly red, tinted with purple bruises; I grabbed him by the collar and threw him as hard as I could down the alleyway. He was too drunk to steady himself and landed on his front, his face torn up a little by the gravel underneath. He looked like he was in the missionary position, just like he had about a year ago.

Piece of shit.

title: Alcohol and Infidelity (short story)
content:
Good looking, yes. What else? Problematic. Attention-seeking. Narcissistic. Selfish. Apparently, she was also irre-fucking-sistible. I’m an idiot. Even recalling it, I want to slash my wrists and dive headfirst through a window, immolate myself and scream until I cough up blood. There really isn’t anything I can look back on with more spite, with more fury, with more regret than this. My blood is boiling just entertaining these thoughts: I will have to be very particular with what I say. I won’t recall how we got together, or why (I don’t think there is a why which is half the problem): rather, I’ll dive right into those moments which lacerated me and left my self-worth pouring out of mental wounds that have now scarred. It’s obvious that it ended, so there’s no point pretending that it’s suspenseful: I eventually found the courage (or intelligence) to end it; only a few months prior to the main narrative, in fact. It was the only relationship I had embarked on since my first one; I took a good year out to savour the sanctity of reflection and making sure I was mentally stable.

And then it took about three days to lose it all.

Picture, if you will, a phone in my hand. It’s three o’ clock in the morning; I’ve just been awoken by a phone call (whose sound now sends shivers down my spine: no wonder I got rid of it). Half-asleep, I’m greeted by the voice of someone very particular. As I listen to her, my mental image is quite clear: blond hair, blue eyes. What else needs to be said about that? I couldn’t get the accurate picture in your head if I tried, so let’s work with that. Drunk, she says ‘I’m so sorry . . . I’ve got something to tell you.’
My heart now racing, palpitating; fearing the worst, I ask, ‘What is it?’

Thorough tears the other end.

‘What is it?’ I repeat.

‘I slept with someone.’

The clock stops ticking. I think my heart stopped beating. Those few seconds where I use my mental cutlery to chop up the linguistic content I’ve just been served, and then dine on each particular syllable, taking it in, then savouring it as a whole . . . those were the last few moments on this planet where I can say I had any wholesome, uninterrupted, positive feelings towards this girl. After that, what? A mixture of hate, self-hate, disdain and confusion.

No one had ever cheated on me before. I had never cheated on anyone. Never will. (And it would take an idiot or a dire waste of oxygen to do so, especially after they’ve been cheated on.)

Infidelity: my curse, my burden, my torturer.

The first and only time a source of depression has ever come externally to me. So why does it feel like I’m being ripped apart from the inside out? Thoughts on fire, I ask banal and meaningless questions:

‘Who? When? . . . Why?’

More tears. More time to wonder about the details. Grimy hands, groping, orgasms. I want to tear someone’s throat out.

Possibly my own.

‘A couple of months ago . . .’

How does that make sense? Why would someone cheat on you and then tell you two months later? I asked her a similar question.

‘I—I was too weak. Too nervous. I needed alcohol in my system.’

The best part was, I’d spent the evening with her before she went out clubbing (for some waste of space’s birthday). What better way to spend an eve than covered in other people’s sweat and your own regret? Apparently none.

Looking for something to say, I keep asking the same questions. ‘Who with?’

She wouldn’t say. ‘Couldn’t’ say – the mark of a liar.

‘Hold on.’ Finally I trace the dates she’s giving me. I almost jump out of bed (where does it matter where I’m sitting or standing, really?): ‘we’ve only be going out for two months . . . What the f—‘

‘I was scared. Scared of falling for you—‘

What a bunch of bullshit.

‘It was . . . two days after we got together.’

Never has a sentence ripped through me with quite such force as that one. Like a bullet, the entry wound was simple and concise: right in the ear. The exit wound, however, was not only brutal to look at – it took me months and months to finally find the fucking bullet and sew up the wound.

Tears start rolling down my face; slowly. Nothing dramatic: there are only a few. But within those few droplets it seems as though the world’s misery has found a home. The clock has stopped ticking. All I can hear is my own lack of breath – my complete breathless shock.

Why? Why all this? If we’d only been together for two months, why not get rid? Well, this perfect example of feminine reasoning had truly sunk her claws in. I could feel them start to tear my flesh as I contemplated pulling them out. In those two months I’d become very involved: I thought it was love. Consider the betrayal: all that time, all of it, she’d been lying to me.
‘Not telling the truth isn’t the same as lying’ is what I heard on the other end of the phone.

I threw mine against the wall.

I think I’ll sit in this position where the news broke for a few hours. I certainly won’t be sleeping. The same soft skin and lips I’d sat and drunk in – well, it was all too late. Someone had already gotten there, said whatever needed to be said to ‘seduce’ (what does that word even mean anymore?) her, and had his way. Three minutes of gritty fucking ecstasy, scraped knees, whimpering sounds, drunken slobbering – and a whole lot of pain for me. All of this had taken place in such a wonderful place. A bed, perhaps? In the lounge of some lothario? No, not quite:

In an alleyway.

*


 All these details came later. All I could get out of her at first was a wonderfully vague story about ‘some guy called Josh’, a ‘tall, dark-haired’ guy who wouldn’t leave her alone. She told him she had a boyfriend but he persisted. Sitting at a table in some club, he eventually leaned in and kissed her: she kissed back. Later, after a few drinks, they found themselves out behind the nightclub having a cigarette. Alone. In the meantime, I was at home probably feeling worldly, philosophising about the mind-body problem – or more realistically, I was wondering how she was doing, what she was up to.

She was too drunk to say no but not drunk enough to make sure he wore a condom. It was ‘forgettable’, or ‘awful’, or whatever the fuck she said – then he walked off and joined his friends whilst she probably lit up a post-coital cigarette.

This is the story I ‘believed’ (though to say I wasn’t sceptical would be a lie) for another year – yes, I stayed with her for a year – until in the final weeks of our relationship when, sitting on a sofa watching some utterly forgettable television programme, the topic randomly flitted through my mind for what must have been the thousandth time.

It turned out her backstory wasn’t even half true. Due to purposeful repression of these events I can’t remember the exact question, but in a matter of seconds I worked out who it was she had had sex with that night: a few seconds later I was standing up almost pulling my hair out; I told her not to come near me but she insisted on trying to hug me as if I was about to leave the planet forever. Luckily, I wasn’t; but that was to be the beginning of the end. My rage got the better of me; a rage that has never been released outside of the sports field or the gym. The results were unpleasant. I messaged the . . . person . . . (of course, she had his number on her phone the whole time – the entire year) and told him what I knew. Obviously, it was quite a while ago: since then he’d had sex with countless numbers of STD-ridden, fake-tan streaked, fake-eyelash dropping girls who dropped their pants before their glass of vodka, so it was probably hard for him to remember which alleyway this was, which blurry human that was on the receiving end of his boy-like frame’s attempt at sexual intercourse.

*


My left hand is around his throat. It’s just he and I in the alleyway; a few weeks after I found out it was he who’d caused all of this. Well, the two of them. Luckily it was a Saturday, so he was out and about, drinking. Not difficult to find. Now he was gasping for air. I can see the sweat run down his arm over the tattoo of his Italian name. He puts both of his hands over mine to try and pull my fingers from the delicate skin on his lightly-stubbled throat which are leaving bruises. I loosen my grip a little before I kill him.

His greasy, short black hair and five-clock shadow make me reflect: I wonder with what passion she kissed him?  I can see the traces of his dimples, the same components of his ‘cheeky chappy’ smile which are distorted with the sobering look of fear that has accosted all of his features. Distress screams out with his features as he struggles for breath.

He’s drunk.

So am I.

I hate alcohol, but I’d been swigging the contents of a square-bottled whiskey jar, neat, all the way here. That’s probably why my grip is so hard: I can’t even hear him squeal. Oh, he just did. It was quite feminine; as if I was dominating him. Oh, I am. I see lipstick at the side of his lips, fading as he continues to sweat.

‘Is that your girlfriend’s?’

He tries to say something but he can’t get the words out. Turns out you need a sufficient opening for your larynx to make words. I take a heart gulp of the whiskey from the bottle in my right hand. It’s about two-thirds of the way finished, so I throw the bottle away and wipe away some of the whiskey which is carelessly trickling down through my beard, which is extremely thick and bedraggled. I’m sweating too, and parts of the fringe from my rather long mid-length hair are sticking to my face. I loosened my grip after repeating my question: I reduced the pressure on his jugular whilst maintaining a thorough and dominating grip around his neck as a whole, to let him know who was in control.

‘Yes,’ he fairly whispered out.

‘Should I go and see her?’ Too menacingly for me. Purely for effect. I couldn’t give a fuck about his girlfriend. She has it bad enough: she thought being with this scumbag would be a good decision. Why would I cause someone like that any further harm? She was doomed already. This isn’t me. But I’m too far in now.

‘Do you know who I am?’

‘No, I don’t – you freak!’

‘Didn’t you get my messages?’ I don’t know how I managed to speak this coolly or clearly.

The flicker of recognition in his eyes: finally, the drunken idiot had put it all together. I could have sworn I felt his body shiver with fear.

‘Well, I said I’d make you pay. You might think you can have sex with whoever the fuck you like . . . but sooner or later someone was going to punish you for complete disregard for everything and everyone other than your own libido.’ He didn’t know what libido meant. ‘Dick. Your dick. You think with your dick.’

Suddenly he had a wave of courage. ‘I know people. I’m out with them right now. Let go of me.’ I obviously wasn’t gripping him hard enough. I pinned his left hand to the wall with my right, dragging his knuckles along the brickwork. I could see from his wincing that it was the right thing to do. He wasn’t striking me with his free hand: if he was, I would have broken it. Somehow, I think he knew that. He knew that I was extremely worked up, if not deranged. Passionate, if not vicious. But I was on the edge between these small inklings of punishment and far more serious one.

‘There’s a reason no one has ever started a fight with me.’ I pulled his cheeks together so his lips were puffed up. He was completely under my control. I could do whatever I wanted. ‘It’s unfortunate that you chose her of all people to sleep with –‘

No, no, that’s not right.

‘”Fuck”, isn’t it? You fucked her. Right?’

No response.

‘That sounds about right. She said it was awful. Not that I care.’ That was a lie. A needless lie. ‘I’m not a killer. I’m not even violent. The funny thing is, I’m a pacifist. But look at me. I’m drunk. I hate drinking. I’ve got some waste of skin pinned to a wall. Look at you! What are you doing with your life? Fucking other people’s girlfriends?’

‘Everyone makes mistakes.’

How true. ‘I’m making a mistake right now.’

‘She treated you like a mug, mate. You should be angry at her, not me,’ he said, trying to loosen my grip – which I duly tightened. On and off. To give him the feeling of being free and then to take it away again.

He was right. What was I doing? I was intoxicated enough to do all this and go against everything I believe in but I wasn’t intoxicated enough to do something I’d really regret. In fact, I wouldn’t regret this at all.

‘If you ever speak my name, think about me, talk about me, tell anyone this happened . . .’

‘I won’t. Just let go of me.’

‘I’m glad you didn’t go for the tough-guy act you seemed to try over the phone. I didn’t believe you. And even if you were a tough guy, what would that matter? Size doesn’t matter. All that matters is passion. Whoever wants to win a fight most, wins. End of. And you have everything to lose. I have nothing left to lose.’ Images flashed back into my head of everything: all the shit I’d put up with for the past year, my own stupidity and weakness, the doubt that had crept into me, the fact I’d chosen such an awful ‘partner’ in the first place. All of this, this wasn’t anger at him: it was anger at me. It was self-destruction through the means of pinning some unintelligent ‘lad’ against a wall and making him fear for his life. I was done with it.

‘Get out of here. Try not to fuck anyone else tonight. Or someone might actually be angry enough to go through with it.’ I released my hand from his throat, which was now thoroughly red, tinted with purple bruises; I grabbed him by the collar and threw him as hard as I could down the alleyway. He was too drunk to steady himself and landed on his front, his face torn up a little by the gravel underneath. He looked like he was in the missionary position, just like he had about a year ago.

Piece of shit.

I wandered off in the other direction, stopping only to look at the whiskey bottle. I spat at it, and promised myself that I would never drink again.

And I didn’t.

title: The Need to Be Original (essay)
content:
The Need to Be Original
By Luke Labern


The aim of this short essay is simply to inspire thought and, perhaps, action.

I


I am currently sitting in a car on a motorway and have decided that rather than spend it in silence looking at the countryside whizzing past, I would write this. This leads directly into my point: the need to be original. My definition of the word ‘original’ is different, depending on the context in which I am using it and what I’m arguing for. At this moment, however, I am thinking of originality as akin to vitality and creativity. I need to, much as this essay is attempting to, provoke thought. To shift the emphasis away from the past and to place, with force, the need for right now to matter. So what if you are not Shakespeare, Mozart, or any genius associated in your field? Even if you are the genius of your profession, you may not know it. It is imperative to have faith both in your abilities (no matter how limited they are) and in your realisation that if the world is going to continue, we must ignore the fact that these people ever lived. I mean this in a nuanced way: of course I do not mean we must forget Shakespeare, but rather we must not let him torture us with his brilliance. Just because he has written Hamlet does not stop you from writing your novel, your play, your poem, your work of art. This is a message not only to artists, however: it is to quite literally everyone.

Creativity and inspiration are not reserved to artists. In every conversation there is need for lucidity and originality. In almost every circumstance you can find yourself in where you have any chance to act freely, there is the chance to affect the world positively and creatively. Every person is individual, as anyone will tell you: and I am not writing this from some misplaced sense of Americanised therapeutic optimism. I am simply stating the fact that every person who can be described accurately through the use of a cliché is failing as a human being. There is within every single person at least one spark of originality, something unique to them which has never before been seen in the whole of humanity. It is your job as a human, I argue, to identify these sparks of originality and to cultivate them. The benefits will give your friends a more interesting life and a sense of pride in knowing you, your parents a source of pride to have given birth to such a ‘wonderful specimen’ and, most persuasively of all, to you.

What will originality bring to you? Perhaps power. Perhaps fame. Perhaps wealth. Even if it doesn’t, however, you will have something to be proud of: a real personality. A depth. A complexity, a secret, a charm – if nothing else, a purpose. And that alone is admirable.

 II

Originality breeds respect.

There is no success without trying.

title: Fossil Fuels (poem)
content:
I made prayers as a child
      To appease selfish wishes --
'Let them be okay,' and 'Please,
      Could I have this and that?'

A child alone believes in fantasy;
      A man, at best, pretends.
The hole in the sky or the hole in the ground:
      That's where it ends.

Isolation begets imagination
      But it also breeds regret:
The longer I live, the more sure I am
      That I live to forget.

Swagger and bravado run through my veins,
      Like precious fossil fuels:
I'm an engine.
      Scrapheap or car crash?

title: Authenticity 1: Goals
content:
What follows is a short section from my novel. It is taken out of context, but it not only stands alone well, as a nice exposition of my personal philosophy, but reveals one of the many flavours of my novel. I hope you enjoy it. The theme of 'authenticity' is key both to my novel and to me, personally, and so I will be posting some more excerpts related to it. I hope you will find them interesting -- even better, inspirational.

* * *

I will start with authenticity.

This is a subject most important to me. In finally plugging the hole which leaked confidence, I began to reassess my position both within the group and within the world itself. What I had lost in the relationship I quickly regained. When I looked in the mirror during that time, I saw a man who wasn’t living up to his own ideals – worst of all, I was a man who was overshadowed by his past. The moment I regained control of my life was the moment I was able to say ‘I’m no longer living in the past: the present is now the most important moment of my life’. Separated both from my friends and myself whilst in that relationship, I became less than half a person. I expended all of my energy trying to hold onto an illogical and ill-fitting relationship and in the process didn’t have enough left over for the necessary amount of work it takes not only to hold oneself together, but to improve oneself.

And self-improvement is the one thing that drives me more than anything else in life.

Philosophy now is often described in terms of a split between ‘continental’ and ‘analytic’ philosophy. I have interests in both areas, but overall, I despise the pathetic dichotomy: philosophy is my secret weapon. It is my passion, my life, my power. It is the one thing that allows me to rise above those who reside in the unoriginal and it is the one singular tool I have that I value most of all. For me, philosophy is the art of reflection without emotion with two principle aims: to assess the questions relating to the meaning of life and the existence of God, and, using the results from the former, learning how to flourish in life. That is, philosophy is the art of living life well. And that is the one thing that I strive to do above all else.

Key to this are the particular schools of philosophy known as existentialism and absurdism (often conflated together, but slightly different). Their antithesis is nihilism. I see the three as all different positions on the same spectrum: where one sits on the spectrum is a result of their beliefs regarding the existence of God, the meaning of life and how life should be lived. When I am depressed, or highly realistic with a pessimistic flavour, I am a heavy nihilist. When I decide that suicide isn’t for me, I turn my efforts towards the other two: my sense of humour stems from my absurdist beliefs. That is, I believe that humans intrinsically search for meaning but that there simply is none. Existentially speaking, I am a firm believer (and proof) that goal-setting is the only way to live and flourish in the twenty-first century. My absurdist tendencies always remind me, though, that my goal must be held at an ironic arm’s length, because regardless, nothing I do in life matters. This allows me to come to peace with certain things – but it also makes me value life more than I ever could if I believed in a God, because I know that this is the only life I am ever going to get. I my one, single tenure on this planet, as this person and no one else – so I am going to enjoy it, rule it and make the most of it. I embrace pain in success – I’ll never be able to feel pain, or anything else, again; I am not afraid of pain. I am not afraid of death. I am afraid of the physical process of dying, but that is because I am a proud man and hate losing. Losing the game of survival will surely be transcendentally awful, but I am utterly resolved to being proud on my death-day.

I will be proud of who I am the day I day: that is why I will not want to die. I never run out of things to do.

The word ‘goal’ itself is unfortunately Americanised to my ears. That accepted, the function of a goal is the single greatest thing a human being can hope for: it is where existentialism and realism meet; where the theoretical and practical marry and the end result is not only productivity (the most important thing of all), but often happiness (I do not value this as the most important thing, but it certainly is vital).

Goals help cut through my philosophical idealism, my many dreams and my romantic notions like a guiding light: a beacon of logic by which to measure my progress as a human being. I set goals with time frames: when the time has elapsed, I’ll know if I’ve failed or not. Even better, I’ll know why and how I failed or succeeded. There’s little better than the feeling of achieving a goal, or dream. There’s also nothing quite as tragic. The moment one achieves their dream, the absurd takes over. You realise that the many hours (months, years, etc.) you spent working towards a goal, often in pain but often in excited anticipation – are over. The few seconds of pleasure you revel in are nothing compared to the struggle. The struggle itself is the beautiful part. You are older You’re a little closer to death. Possibly perilously close. The most tragic thing of all is achieving your life’s goal: when you achieve that, something truly unique happens.

Your life ends.

If you dream of one thing obsessively for decades (my example being my passion for writing) and achieve it: what then? You will never again – in your entire life – want something as much as that dream. From that point on, just like a serious drug user, you will be ‘chasing the high’ – never achieving it again. Once life begins, it’s all downhill from there. We are born terminally ill. Yet the truly strong, truly creative, truly original human being accepts all of this. One simply makes new goals: more ambitious than the last.

I am the man I am because of these beliefs. Because I realise my life is, in the strictest sense of the word (cosmologically, statistically) meaningless, I am able to make the most of my life. If I was to reveal my most cherished dreams and goals, I would most likely be called insane and shunned by society, or called narcissistic and delusional. And yet, it is by aiming at my over-arching, grand goals that I have made all the process I have done in my life.

I know the way to my grand goals: I know they are possible. I know that by achieving every one of my smaller goals, these existential stepping stones will lead me down the path I want to follow. At the end of the road is death, but hopefully posterity. Quite simply, at the end of it all, I want to have made an impact on the world. I want to be considered a great writer and a great person. I want to be considered great, full stop.

I have thought long and hard about whether I ever wanted to write that down and let it enter the public domain, but I have decided that to lie, or pretend that I don’t believe what I believe, would be a waste of life and a complete contradiction. I would rather be deluded than a hypocrite. Yes: in bearing myself completely as I am doing now, I am achieving true authenticity.
It’s this authenticity, this openness with my goals, that has allowed me to achieve the status I have amongst friends. If I fail to achieve them, then every critic that ever opened their mouth to spew bile at me is justified. If I succeed, let them be silenced forevermore. I am seen as a inspiration to some, as a leader, as original, as creative – I love all of these adjectives. They give me the passion to carry on in a world which could quite easily consume me and tear me to shreds. Indeed, I would be the one to tear myself apart: there is no in-between: one either hates oneself, or loves themselves. One is either confident or depressed. ‘Numbness’ is a temporary state, usually chemically induced.

At the end of it all, at the heart of it all, you are either with yourself or against yourself.

I am thoroughly with myself: and for that reason I have what some people have called ‘followers’ – I call them peers. I call them my friends, my family. I have been described as ‘romantic’ and ‘dramatic’; I can understand why I have been called these things. I am very much a believer in intensity: my feelings towards things can almost universally be described in terms of love and hate. I do not have time for indecision. My life is short. My goals are certain. My success is in the balance.

Only resolve, action, effort and determination can fulfil my ambition. Powered by drive, I must burn through life ignoring the comments of those who I know I will never be friends with, and fight on both for my own dignity and dreams and also to inspire those around me.

There is no meaning of life.

I live my life as if my created meaning is the only one that matters. That is authenticity.

What else can I do?

Either that, or nothing.

Either live, or die.

One simply makes new goals: more ambitious than the last.

I am the man I am because of these beliefs. Because I realise my life is, in the strictest sense of the word (cosmologically, statistically) meaningless, I am able to make the most of my life. If I was to reveal my most cherished dreams and goals, I would most likely be called insane and shunned by society, or called narcissistic and delusional. And yet, it is by aiming at my over-arching, grand goals that I have made all the process I have done in my life.

I know the way to my grand goals: I know they are possible. I know that by achieving every one of my smaller goals, these existential stepping stones will lead me down the path I want to follow. At the end of the road is death, but hopefully posterity. Quite simply, at the end of it all, I want to have made an impact on the world. I want to be considered a great writer and a great person. I want to be considered great, full stop.

I have thought long and hard about whether I ever wanted to write that down and let it enter the public domain, but I have decided that to lie, or pretend that I don’t believe what I believe, would be a waste of life and a complete contradiction. I would rather be deluded than a hypocrite. Yes: in bearing myself completely as I am doing now, I am achieving true authenticity.
It’s this authenticity, this openness with my goals, that has allowed me to achieve the status I have amongst friends. If I fail to achieve them, then every critic that ever opened their mouth to spew bile at me is justified. If I succeed, let them be silenced forevermore. I am seen as a inspiration to some, as a leader, as original, as creative – I love all of these adjectives. They give me the passion to carry on in a world which could quite easily consume me and tear me to shreds. Indeed, I would be the one to tear myself apart: there is no in-between: one either hates oneself, or loves themselves. One is either confident or depressed. ‘Numbness’ is a temporary state, usually chemically induced.

At the end of it all, at the heart of it all, you are either with yourself or against yourself.

I am thoroughly with myself: and for that reason I have what some people have called ‘followers’ – I call them peers. I call them my friends, my family. I have been described as ‘romantic’ and ‘dramatic’; I can understand why I have been called these things. I am very much a believer in intensity: my feelings towards things can almost universally be described in terms of love and hate. I do not have time for indecision. My life is short. My goals are certain. My success is in the balance.

Only resolve, action, effort and determination can fulfil my ambition. Powered by drive, I must burn through life ignoring the comments of those who I know I will never be friends with, and fight on both for my own dignity and dreams and also to inspire those around me.

There is no meaning of life.

I live my life as if my created meaning is the only one that matters. That is authenticity.

What else can I do?

Either that, or nothing.

Either live, or die.

Separated both from my friends and myself whilst in that relationship, I became less than half a person. title: Authenticity 2: The difference between drug use & abuse
content:
If by focusing on what matters to me, regardless of its unusual nature, impact or ability to generate controversy, that garners me authenticity, then that must be what matters most. This leads me to the most prevalent reason explaining why human beings are not authentic: they cannot bear to be themselves in a world which rewards homogeneity with security, the concept of ‘fitting in’. For many, it offers a way to slipstream through life in a pre-establish rote: those who believe they are standing out are usually non-conformist conformists – perhaps the worst of the lot. I commend their spirit, but their execution is clearly lacking. Dying one’s hair, piercing their body and wearing a certain type of clothing liberates no one. The only liberation can come from action and thought.

That is where I stand out.

I need not explain why I stand out: in the process of writing this, I am doing exactly that, by outlining my philosophy – it just so happens that my philosophy is based on promoting the art of philosophising to the position of God.

Such controversial words highlight the point: I know that in being authentic, in truly being myself, in working out what I believe (for example, that God does not exist, and that I must craft my own meaning in life, and that I only have this one, temporary lifetime) I will gain both followers and critics. The case in point is the subject of this book: the difference between drug use and abuse. Some people believe there is no such thing as ‘sensible drug use’ – likely because they have been affected by addiction or the drug world in some admittedly horrible way. My point has been, and always will be, that every single person in the world has a relationship with drugs. Whether one chooses to take them once, every time, or never, they are engaging with something which is a universal feature of the human condition. It is these universal features of human experience that truly fascinate and drive me, so let me delve into this topic a little further.

How can I claim that everyone has a relationship with drugs? Well, consider this: the heroin user, the coffee drinker, the cigarette inhaler, the lager drinker, the prescription medication taker, the marijuana smoker and the LSD tripper all have one thing in common: they are altering their mind and/or body through the use of a chemical external to their body. The chemical they knowingly take changes their brain and they experience a high or a low – in short, an effect. No one would dispute this: this is a fact. And yet, it’s as if people pretend not to know this – when in reality, they shake their head, their cup of tea or coffee in their hand, watching on the news a story about a heroin addict. The only difference is the drug itself. The user is a human: a human who wants to change their life for a temporary period of time.

This is my first justification of my drug use – and my advocating that people using drugs if they want to, and can reason effectively that doing so will be beneficial. It rests on the logical fact that the majority of people that exist take drugs not just sometimes, but often. Most, every single day. Cigarettes. Alcohol. Painkillers. Coffee. Cannabis. Drugs.

The second point is a more philosophical argument, which I’ll arrive at after first distinguishing between the words ‘use’ and ‘abuse’. The key issue is legality: something which is fraught with a crooked history, smeared by political intention and not at all based on scientific, statistical or anecdotal fact. Firstly, the idea that certain drugs do not have medicinal qualities (cannabis, MDMA, LSD) is a disgusting fallacy. This immediately rules out their being a schedule 1 drug in America and a Class A in Britain. These classifications state that the drug in question has no possible use in medicine and is strictly a risk to any and all users. This is a lie. LSD has proven that alcoholics thought beyond repair can stem their addiction; cannabis keeps many millions of people calm every day (far more than are distressed or made paranoid by smoking it) and aids suffers of MS and cancer, and MDMA has almost universally beneficial effects on those who use it in a therapeutic setting (PTSD especially) – the subject of using MDMA responsibly is something I hope I have already shed some light on. It is an invaluable tool.

There are, of course, certain drugs which are entirely no good: methamphetamine, heroin, crack cocaine (and, personally, cocaine falls under this category for me, though this white powder fuels many of the ‘scenes’ in the world behind the scenes from music to business) and others of this destructive sort are vicious parasites. I include alcohol and nicotine in this category too, though I know people will disagree with me. Still, I believe only in those drugs which can aid life without destroying it: caffeine, cannabis, MDMA, LSD (used responsibly). Yes, this word ‘responsibly’ is the key one. Which brings me to my next point:

Most of these drugs are illegal because it is thought that people do not know how to use them responsibly. Politicians will scoff at the term ‘medicinal use’ of cannabis. Why? They seem to believe they can medicate responsibly with over-the-counter painkillers, caffeine, cigarettes and the like. The truth of the matter is that no one has ever died from sole cannabis use. Ever. Yet thousands (millions?) die worldwide due to the misuse of paracetamol, cigarette and alcohol. Possibly even from normal use.

Give me one good reason why cigarettes and alcohol should be legal but cannabis shouldn’t, based on this distinction between users not knowing what’s right for them.

I hope that it is becoming clear that the link between authenticity and drug use is this: I know that my views are controversial, and that my use of drugs is deemed illegal by the society I live in. Yet I stand by what I do, not simply because I am a po-faced, ignorant rebel acting for the sake of it, but because I not only have these reasons, but because I believe I am entitled to. I could obey laws which are pointless and will eventually be repealed, or I could be true to my own beliefs and make the most of my one life.

Authenticity is centred on a focus on death.

Mortality is the key distinguisher, for me, between man and animals. A human knows that it is going to die eventually: it thus plans its life accordingly. There is a sombre sense of doom, but true authenticity is in the act of rebelling against one’s impending death by living life with such passionate vigour that one really is living for the moment. The point is: why live someone else’s life? Why be anyone else than yourself? Even if it causes ridicule, embarrassment, disgust, controversy? At the end of your life, there is no pearly gates judgement: there is simply death. Authenticity occurs in living life as if you were the only person who matters: this may seem naïve, but in reality, everyone values their friends and family as much as they do themselves – in doing what you really want and being who you really want to be, this almost certainly includes making your friends and family proud. Why pretend that you fit the cookie-cutter mould of any stereotype?

You were never a part of history, never a part of the world before you were born – so why should it know how to categorise it? Categorise yourself. Category: you. Population: one.

This is what I do: love me or hate me for it. Honestly, it doesn’t matter in the end.

Authenticity, though, is the first step on a most complicated journey. That journey is life. Authenticity simply guarantees that the right person – the truest version of you -- makes the journey. I believe the journey, regardless of the pitfalls and tests therein, is easier if one is at peace with oneself. It doesn’t guarantee happiness – a naïve and short-sighted inference. All it guarantees is pride and confidence when one returns to the issue of authenticity and realises that they are staying true to who they are. Pride and confidence, in my opinion, are more important than happiness.

There is a sombre sense of doom, but true authenticity is in the act of rebelling against one’s impending death by living life with such passionate vigour that one really is living for the moment. The point is: why live someone else’s life? Why be anyone else than yourself? Even if it causes ridicule, embarrassment, disgust, controversy? At the end of your life, there is no pearly gates judgement: there is simply death. Authenticity occurs in living life as if you were the only person who matters: this may seem naïve, but in reality, everyone values their friends and family as much as they do themselves – in doing what you really want and being who you really want to be, this almost certainly includes making your friends and family proud. Why pretend that you fit the cookie-cutter mould of any stereotype?

You were never a part of history, never a part of the world before you were born – so why should it know how to categorise it? Categorise yourself. Category: you. Population: one.

This is what I do: love me or hate me for it. Honestly, it doesn’t matter in the end.

Authenticity, though, is the first step on a most complicated journey. That journey is life. Authenticity simply guarantees that the right person – the truest version of you -- makes the journey. I believe the journey, regardless of the pitfalls and tests therein, is easier if one is at peace with oneself. It doesn’t guarantee happiness – a naïve and short-sighted inference. All it guarantees is pride and confidence when one returns to the issue of authenticity and realises that they are staying true to who they are. Pride and confidence, in my opinion, are more important than happiness.

title: A Is For Alienation (poem)
content:
A piece of me is stuck with you.
That's fact. There's nothing I can do.
The choice is yours: do what you will:
Nourish -- inflame -- cultivate -- spill.

Psychological geography
Dictates the space between you and me.
Now there's a physical space too --
Yet again, there's nothing I can do.

Left behind -- hold down the fort -- wait.
Separation of mate from mate.
'True love'? I've a few things to say --
But you'll have to wait another day.

I hibernate necessarily:
Need to close my eyes -- too much to see.
Is ignorance bliss? I lie
And lay in bed. Awake. Alone. I.

title: An Existential Eulogy (short story)
content:
This is another extract from my novel. It occurs in the third of four parts. I don't think it'll ruin the story; however, it does perfectly highlight the philosophical and highly original nature of the work, the intensity of emotions involved and the passion I have. I hope, most of all, that it is enjoyable.

If someone taking MDMA at a funeral and giving a eulogy offends you, look away now.

* * *

The day I saw that notebook was about four days after I found out that she died. A week after that day of discovery and ruin it was her funeral. I had never been to a funeral before. Madeline’s mother found out that I was a writer and asked me if I would write – not a eulogy – but a piece of writing to commemorate her for her friends. A chance to redeem myself? If only.

 

There I was, having written the little thing only a few hours before, dressed all in black – the coffin was there, everything was pristine. The usual scene: the small group of people all immaculately dressed on a verdant green (ironically alive grass, I always thought), the women with their odd veils and all of that, the men standing awkwardly around trying to console the women crying. The close friends most distraught of all – these the people truly affected by it. Madeline’s little brother clung to her mother’s leg, not knowing what was going on. I was there, waiting in the wings, as it were. Here I was, the most outspoken atheist in my town here, at a religious funeral, to give an informal eulogy. It was an outside funeral – that is, there was a little podium for the speakers offset, to the left, from the coffin. The priest sat offset to the right and there were some decorations, little wreathes. All very neat, all pristine, organised, prepared.

 

Then there was me. Looking at the paper in my hands, I skimmed over some of the words. I wondered if they’d do – I decided to be respectful. I had originally declined but the mother wanted ‘someone with poetic sensibilities’ and I knew that I could deliver on that front. I had tried to weave something respectful, not too aggressive on the religion side, but most of all, something to honour Madeline. She liked my poetry and encouraged me whenever we spoke. I was doing this for.
Unfortunately, I wasn’t able to do it sober.
The priest began saying the same usual things: ‘We are gathered here today . . .’ and my hand involuntarily found its way into my pocket and fondled a small object. I slowly pulled out the banana pill and slipped it into my mouth, bursting with shame. I wanted to run away. I wish none of it had ever happened. Why couldn’t she just still be alive? Why couldn’t things just be normal? I had no problems with normal? Why did someone have to go and die?

 
A series of speakers began to say the usual kind things and then it was my turn. Just before I was called up – the physiological boom happened; I was sucked into the ecstasy high.

 
The same pressure as always was applied to me, together with instant euphoria and comfort. Disgusting? Yes; but suddenly this speech became the most important thing in the world to me. I was sweating a little as the pill took hold of me. I was never going to smile: that wasn’t part of it. The euphoria was subtle. It was more . . . I can handle this; I can live. It was one of the oddest moments of my life. To see a sea of forlorn faces and to be in that state – that philosophical state. It will stay with me until the day I die. I realised the position of power I was in and stood up on the podium, laying the sheets of paper out in front of me. I looked at what I had written and I realised it wouldn’t suit the occasion. I looked at the speech theatrically and put it back into my pocket. Immediately, I spoke from the heart.

 
‘People always say the same things when they eulogise. They say ‘she would never hurt a fly, she was a kind soul, she was studious’ – all of those sort of things. I suppose that’s because to make the process of a funeral as formulaic as possible allows people to numb themselves: to anaesthetise themselves to their loss. I need to be honest: I’ve never been to a funeral before. I also need to admit that Madeline and I didn’t always see eye to eye – in fact, we fell out quite a lot.

 
‘But that doesn’t matter. Death is death. Her loss has affected me so profoundly that I can honestly say that it’s changed my life. The last time I saw her we sat and spoke in that church over there. We discussed our dreams, our lives, our tumultuous past, to some degree, and we also discussed religion. I’m sorry that you didn’t realise that I was an atheist, Mrs H. – but I promise that doesn’t matter. I’m not going to stand here and talk about any of that. The fact is, we have all suffered a terrible loss. Whether or not you think there is an afterlife, the point is that we are still here in this life. This is what matters. We are all going to have to deal with the loss of this girl . . . in different ways. Some better than others. Never uniformly.

 
‘I know that Madeline wouldn’t have wanted people to stand here and lie and say that she would ‘never hurt a fly’ (no offence to those who have just spoken), or anything like that. The truth is that I doubt she thought much about her funeral. Why would she? She was young and healthy. Vibrant, passionate, driven. She would have wanted someone to stand here and to really say it how it is: so that’s what I’m going to do.’

 
I realised that I was going on quite a bit – I was getting extremely carried away. I made a sideways glance to the priest, who I heard splutter when I mentioned that I was an atheist, but by now was intrigued by me; then I looked at Madeline’s mother and noticed the shock in her face. She saw that I was after her permission and, welling up, she nodded that I should continue. I made a quick pass over Madeline’s other friends and they were all very upset; at the back I noticed K--- and K-----. They gave me a thumbs up. I continued.

 
‘Madeline not only wouldn’t hurt a fly – she did. In fact, she hurt me. But only because I hurt her. This isn’t the point, I know: but she would have wanted the truth. Just like any human, she was capable of true kindness and beauty and also quite capable of being spiteful. Does that make her death in any way easier? No – it makes it harder. She perfectly embodied what it was to be a human. She was curious, intelligent, creative, thoughtful, funny, passionate, emotional, vicious, prone to love, a lot like I am, and always very careful with her moral decisions. Of course she made mistakes. That’s what made her so interesting and vital.’

 
A single tear slowly ran down my cheek.

 

‘I will miss her. You will miss her. We will all miss her. But for every cliché that I have tried to transcend, there is one that I believe will ring true more than any other: it is better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all. Though we are very much burdened now, I still believe – and I know you do too – that it is better that we got to experience her, every single part of her . . . than to have never known her. If she gave you just one memory, or affected you for just one moment; made you frustrated even briefly, or gave you a single laugh – she has not only affected your life, she is now forever a part of life. You can never erase the past. And that means you can never erase her.

 
‘She will, of course, remain only in photographs and memories now. I know that, personally, I will shed many more tears – and probably lots worse – but despite it all, I take nothing back. Would I rather she be alive? Of course. Would I rather she be here even if I never got to speak to or see her again? Undoubtedly. She was a human: she was original, intuitive, philosophical and more than anything, authentic. I am glad to have known her. I would do almost anything to see her back: I wish death on no one. Whilst I know she would definitely hurt a fly – I know that she would never wish death on anyone else, either.

 
‘That I have to use the past tense makes this a tragedy. I don’t try to hide that fact: we are, all of us, in for an extremely difficult time. Perhaps some of us will never truly recover, haunted by everything that was. But you know what? Madeline would have wanted us to laugh and enjoy life. She was religious – but she, like me, like all of us – knew that life is precious regardless of our beliefs. She would not want her demise to ruin our temporary moments on this earth. How we will all grieve is not my business: I know that I can barely control my own. I am merely saying what I know she would have wanted to say. I knew her intimately and in various capacities – but I know that quite honestly, this is what she would have wanted to say:

 
‘Don’t let my death stop you from living.

 
‘Honestly? I’d rather it was me in that coffin and her standing here. Her passion has always been incredibly beautiful to me – just one facet of a wonderfully complex person. I’m sorry for saying all of this – I didn’t mean to stand here and take up so much of your time. I will finish as soon as I have read this poem which I wrote a long time ago.’

 
Everyone was in stunned silence – I had no idea of what was going on around me; I was in the middle of an MDMA trip and had been possessed. I had managed to channel what I had wanted to without any regards for the situation or what was needed. I had no idea of what the response was, or was supposed to be, but I didn’t care. I held back the rest of my tears and said, in a broken, quiet voice, these lines which I had written in a completely different context, but which fitted the moment perfectly:

 

And I will miss you, when you leave.
Our time spent will never be lost:
But there will be tears on my sleeve --
Missing you, my heart turns to frost.


Where once was heated, now is chill'd:
Have you left, before I say this?
My loving spirit -- it was fill'd...
Now only in memory do you exist.


But to know that you're content
Wherever it is that you are
With or without my selfish consent...
Leaves fresh wounds that I know will scar.


Now I know that I'll be alone.
The brevity of our loving
Shows me that I'll never atone.
I, stationary, whilst you are moving.


Young, innocent beauty squandered
On none, when you are so desired.
The time I spent -- How I pondered!
The grain gone: yet you're still admired.


And I will miss you, when you leave.
Our time spent will never be lost:
But there will be tears on my sleeve --
Missing you, my heart turns to frost.


 I finished reading the poem (the one part of the original speech I used), nodded to her mother and immediately walked off stage, through the graveyard and far away from the funeral, tears accompanying me all the way.

title: B Is For Bitterness (poem)
content:
Ah, rightly wronged. What's worse
Than waiting patiently
For misery? Modern curse;
Weakness of mine most patently.

Well watch the clock and wait
Wait
      Wait
            Wait
                  Wait
Fret.
Don't worry, don't think, don't sweat.

Too late. I lost it all
Again. So I sink
And slither home, upset and appalled.
Why can't I control what I think?

I foresee misery
But can't prevent it.
So I become most miserly.
So, I guess you'll . . .

I said I guess you'll . . .

I guess you'll have to deal with my shit.

title: C Is For Cauterisation (poem)
content:
I

A slit vein will leak:
That much is clear.
A beating heart will bleed;
Truths need not breed fear.

Yes: I panic for the sake of it
To feel alive
Awkward palpitations
Can't sleep tonight

Won't sleep tonight
But that's okay
Can't die in my sleep
If it's all one day.

Isolation defines me
But I grow old.
A piece of me shrinks
When the bed grows cold.

II

Would I do it again
(The mistakes, the pain,
The heartbreak)?
I can't.

I don't believe in second chances
Or God
Or afterlife
Or objectivity

What's done is done --
We all have our scars.
Don't know if we deserve it, but
The world is ours.

We can earn it -- if
We keep our nerves calm
And our morals stuff
-- Palm in palm.

III

Could we go it alone?
For a while, I think.
Why try? What's the point
In a half-empty throne?

The king has been bleeding:
Seven veins he struck.
Whose advice is he heeding?
His own, with any luck.

Isn't destruction twice
As worse
When the mirror's reflection
Is driving the hearse?

Suicide postponed
For many a year.
No guarantees --
Playing it by ear.

IV

As long as I have
What I need
I won't give in to
Self-destructive greed.

But if they take
Her -- and that --
And this
I'll strike again -- and I won't miss.

Please stop bleeding.
It won't seem to clot.
The question is --
To be, or to be not?

I'm saying 'to be'
Because you exist.
For that reason alone
I'll cauterise this:

My jugular remains
So long as you love
The blood in these veins.

title: Power Hungry (sonnet)
content:
The "powerful" are the weakest of men.
    To those who strive - and sweat - and strain - to seem
The strongest -- I hereby wield this pen
    To cross through your hypocritical sheen;
Non-punctuated as your writing is,
    I hope literacy allows you this:
Tone down your voice and mind your business.
    Superiority your parti pris?
No: only the quiet should be listened to.
    Those who abuse their voice (and my ears)
Live clichéd lives and leave me more work to do.
    Your putrid dreams become my greatest fears:
        The powerful seem thus because they hide --
        The truly great stay strong with silent pride.

No: only the quiet should be listened to.
    Those who abuse their voice (and my ears)
Live clichéd lives and leave me more work to do.
    Your putrid dreams become my greatest fears:
        The powerful seem thus because they hide --
        The truly great stay strong with silent pride.

title: The Contradictory Nature of God (Part I)
content:
This is part one of an essay I have been planning to write for a few weeks. It is a strictly philosophical essay, though I will move in and out of the usual philosophical parlance in order to communicate with my audience in a more general way. It will concern a number of topics: omniscience, omnibenevolence, etc., and other issues with the ontological argument and so on. It is written from an atheistic point of view, but is purposefully not dogmatic. It is intended to clarify debate on the topic and to provoke thought -- not to offend or convert.

Part I is an introduction and a short overview of the problems I have found with the philosophy of religion (unfortunately, I am only accustomed with the christian/Western tradition -- I make this 'bias' clear here, as it is my 'area of expertise'). I do hope you comment either here or via facebook and twitter -- get involved, I'd love to know your thoughts.



I
The problem with essays on the philosophy of religion


 

God is often described as omnipotent, omniscient and omnibenevolent. ‘He’ is also described in various other ways – some claim that ‘He’ has necessary existence, is perfect in every way and cares about our lives – others quibble about the details and instead maintain that there is simply such a thing but that he is unknowable.

This essay will be a critique on what I see as the vacuous (at best) or arrogant claims from believers who not only think (“know”) that there is a God, but that ‘He’ is all sorts of things: all-powerful, all-knowing, all-good, for example. There are, of course, infinitely many varieties of these claims – it would be impossible to explore all of them. Thus, I will be concerning myself with some of the major ones that are presented to me in the Western tradition of belief. I hope that those whose conception of God is not directly addressed by this essay do not merely wipe their brow and continue blindly, having felt a bullet passed them by – I intend for these readers to apply the same sort of thinking on their own conception and question what they really “know” – and how much of it is guesswork (or, worse, random designation of certain attributes to this higher power of theirs).



I will begin by explain my reasons for doing this – for going over ground that has been gone over many times before. It seems to me that when discussing, for example, the so-called ‘arguments’ for God, it is largely Christian philosophers of religion (“theologians”) who write the most widely-read theses. This is inevitable, but from my own studies I have found there to be a serious error in the entire school of the philosophy of religion. Throughout their articles (I am here referring mainly to philosophers of religion in the analytic tradition who explore various arguments for God and his nature) they display their great prowess, their adept use of logical arguments, incisively cutting swathes through ambiguities and highlight the issues in a beautiful way. However, time after time – in every single article I have read – there comes a point when their “faith” seeps into the piece and the sustained focus they have maintained throughout, in undoing the arguments of other philosophers unravels. Often, it is something as simple as ‘God being perfect . . .’ – which seems harmless enough.

In reality, this is exactly the sort of unthinking use of language that they pick others up on but seem to hypocritically ignore when it is they who introduce bias without justification. Whilst we could grant them that God is perfect, as a premise, to allow their argument to build – they never highlight that such a premise might be contentious. They take it as given that the reader (whether religious, anti-religious or apathetic) agrees that God would be perfect (or all-good, all-knowing, etc.). The point is that not only is this rare – it is impossible. The philosophers here are indulging their own egoistic and idiosyncratic form of belief and are burdening the reader with their own views which the reader neither wants nor appreciates – certainly in my case.

 

I am, indeed, an atheist. I am also, however, completely open-minded. I question my beliefs as often as I possibly can without losing my sense of identity. If God reveals “him”self to me, or is in any way proven, I will be the first to renounce my mistake and commit to whatever it is “He” wants me to do. But this article is not intended to turn believers into atheists – it is simply an explanation into what is described as ‘the nature of God’. I will let it be known at the outset that I do not think the human mind could ever know the nature of God – man does not even know himself. This needs no justification except recourse to experience. Show me the man who says he truly knows himself and I will show you a liar.

 

This essay, then, is simply an attempt to explore some important question into how and why people believe in God. I hope it will be interesting and thought-provoking to believers, agnostics and atheists alike. I am sure that many will have spotted the irony in that I have been making use of idiosyncratic punctuation without justifying it – this was all for effect, I assure you.

I have placed certain terms within sardonic quotation marks because I wanted to highlight the problem with discussion about religion. It is taken for granted by many that God is “He”. This is an inheritance from the Christian religion. This is the first of my problems with essays on the philosophy of religion: I will use the example of atheists, because I am one, but the point remains for other non-Christian.

 

I am aware of my own context: as a Briton alive in the twenty-first century, it is explainable why the term “He” is a common referent for God, as the United Kingdom is inherently a Christian one (although it is increasingly secular – but this is another topic altogether). But if we are to debate religious subject-matter responsibly, I cannot allow myself to fall into tradition or habit – at any point. It seems to be obvious that if there was a God, “He” would not be a “He” at all – why would a higher power of any sort be considered in terms of gender? Why not give him an age, an ethnicity or a sub-culture too? It seems incredibly short-sighted to attribute human features to God.

 

This is controversial in itself, I realise – thus, I will clarify: I accept that God’s existence is possible, and during this essay I will specifically ‘believe’ in God, or propose that “He” does exist – but in doing so, I will be exploring those features of “Him” that seem acceptable to give to “Him”. A human nature is not one of them. Bearing in mind that humans did not exist for millions of years since the beginning of time, and that it is more than likely, statistically-speaking, that there is other life on planets in other universes, throughout the history of “time” (an admittedly human concept), it seems ferociously arrogant to me to assume that God is in any way related to humans. That alone will forever stop me conceiving God as a “Him”, a “Her” or an old man with a beard. This issue being raised, I will consider it at more length in the next section – the function of this is merely to highlight the tenuous use of the word “He” when referring to God. I will be no longer be using this system of quotation and will refer to God as “it” or some other gender-neutral term.

 

On, then, to the common (mis)conceptions of God’s nature.

title: A Genius Insomniac, A Genius Asleep (poem)
content:
Some call it the cousin of death
Whilst others long for a lie-in;
I change my mind with every breath --
"A waste," when awake -- but lying,
I find myself in earthly bliss --
Free to explore philosophic
Fancy, whether sharp or remiss --
The joy of a life diastolic.

But what torture is sleeplessness!
Tossing, turning, thinking, yearning
Of could have beens -- true restlessness:
Foe to peace of mind and learning.
No good can come from a poor night's sleep;
Just misery and tired bones.
Always at night our fears will creep
And play sly melancholy tones.

I dread the inevitable times
That I become insomniac.
As sure as these successives rhymes
I'm proven no hypochondriac.
A mind thus wired for success
Necessitates wide eyes at night:
These whirring cogs I must suppress --
I'll save penetrative thoughts till light.

(The lights are out -- I'm whispering:
Sleepy now -- hope you're listening --
Know that genius never sleeps:
In dreams, a genius makes leaps!
A genius alone knows this:
Sleep truly is pure earthly bliss.)

title: On Looking at My Lover's Face (poem)
content:
To Georgia.

An eyebrow traced across your face
    Defines your existence thus:
Arching and delicately laced
    With moral strength and trust.

That such a simple undulation
    Contains your total essence
Necessitates this exclamation:
    You, Beauty's quintessence.

They say that poetry is dead:
    Well, let them waste their breath --
Your face alone will do instead.
    You alone ward off death.

Smoothest skin, features perfect;
    A most disarming smile --
Are you the subject -- or object
    Of beauty? Let's think awhile:

"Beauty is subjective," you say --
    Well so too is life's meaning,
But life is already underway.
    Now for poetic gleaning:

Subjective it may be, but still
    We live though this were false:
Your beauty is permanent, and still --
    Regardless time or pulse.

How -- how can I argue like this?
    After much meditation:
The point, I'm sure, no one will miss:
    Here lies adoration.

title: On Looking at My Lover's Face (poem)
content:
To Georgia.

An eyebrow traced across your face
    Defines your existence thus:
Arching and delicately laced
    With moral strength and trust.

That such a simple undulation
    Contains your total essence
Necessitates this exclamation:
    You, Beauty's quintessence.

They say that poetry is dead:
    Well, let them waste their breath --
Your face alone will do instead.
    You alone ward off death.

Smoothest skin, features perfect;
    A most disarming smile --
Are you the subject -- or object
    Of beauty? Let's think awhile:

"Beauty is subjective," you say --
    Well so too is life's meaning,
But life is already underway.
    Now for poetic gleaning:

Subjective it may be, but still
    We live though this were false:
Your beauty is permanent, and still --
    Regardless time or pulse.

How -- how can I argue like this?

The point, I'm sure, no one will miss:
    Here lies adoration.

Yes: your eyebrows, your eyes, your form
    Are great aesthetic gifts --

    Is precisely in this:

Though your timeless, beautiful face
    Is where I did begin --
The secret to your infinite grace
    Is that it is within.
